items.title: What's New in SAP Convergent Charging 2025 FPS2
items.author: AbhijeetDhar
items.text:
New Release 
 PUBLIC 

 October 2026 
 Dear Convergent Charging and BRIM community, 
 We are pleased to announce that SAP Convergent Charging 2025 FPS2 became generally available on October 21st, 2026. This release brings a brand-new RESTful Rating Service for stateless price calculation, introduction of Scope Item 85V for Consumption based charging with SAP CC, enhanced user management model empowering single user holds different roles across multiple clients, and many other exciting new features. 
 Let's dive into these latest product features in detail highlighting our latest pricing and charging capabilities, as part of the SAP Billing and Revenue Innovation Management (BRIM) suite . 
 RESTful Rating Service 
 Imagine you are building a bid management system for a logistics company where you need to calculate parcel shipping fees in real time, well before a contract is created, so that you can show the customer what the actual shipping cost would be. In another case, consider a cart management scenario where prices must be displayed as items are added, long before the customer commits to the purchase. In both scenarios, you need to calculate fees against a charge plan or rate plan without requiring a contract. However, until FPS2, SAP CC supported rating only through the CC Core SDK, making it less suitable for lightweight, REST-based integrations. 
 With FPS2, SAP CC introduces the RESTful Rating Service (v1) , a new stateless REST API that computes fees directly against a charge plan or rate plan without requiring the contract involved. 
 The service introduces two new operations to address these key scenarios: 
 `POST /rest/rating/v1/chargeableItemRate` for event-based usage, and 
 `POST /rest/rating/v1/contractEventRate` for all contract events in a validity period. 
 The rating result is returned to the caller as response items containing configurable fields, which can be sent back to the calling system (such as an API client or bid management application) as informational feedback, without creating any billing records. 
 The API is published on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub. 
 In addition, the current release delivers Version 2 of the existing Charging REST Service. Thus, charging goes one step further than rating: it not only computes fees but also posts them against a contract, resulting in the creation of billing records. 
 With Charging Service v2, the API terminology is also aligned with that of the new Rating Service, providing developers with consistent experience across both services. 
 Benefits: 
 Supports price calculation use cases without requiring a charging contract. 
 Enables executing the rating process without using the CC Core SDK. 
 Charging Service v2 aligns its terminology with the new Rating Service, ensuring a consistent API experience across both services 
 For more information: Rating REST Service 
 Also available: Rating Service on SAP Business Accelerator Hub 
 Scope Item 85V 
 As modern businesses shift toward dynamic, usage-based services, managing complex monetization processes has become a major operational challenge. As more customers adopt SAP CC, establishing end-to-end integration with the BRIM landscape from scratch can be challenging and resource-intensive. 
 With the current release, we are excited to introduce Scope Item 85V (Consumption-Based Charging with SAP Convergent Charging) , which addresses this challenge by providing a preconfigured, scalable foundation for implementing subscription-based business models. It integrates subscription order management with automated usage rating, while enabling seamless integration with Convergent Invoicing and FI-CA for usage and master data replication. 

 [Figure 1: Process Navigator for Scope Item 85V: Consumption Based Charging with SAP CC] 
 The current release supports the initial master data setup across BRIM, integration and master data replication to SAP CC, and includes a sample Rate Plan to help customers get started. Replication of usage-rated consumption for billing purposes is planned for the next release. 
 With this integration in place, customers can establish a consistent subscription lifecycle, from subscription order creation and provider contract replication to charge calculation. It ensures that subscription orders, provider contracts, and rate plans remain aligned across SOM, SAP CC, and FI-CA, providing a scalable foundation for delivering and managing subscription-based and consumption-driven services. 
 For more information refer – Process Navigator , and Help page 
 Detailed blog on the scope Item - Scope Item 85V – Consumption-Based Charging with SAP Convergent Charging 
 Individual User Multiple Client Assignment 
 Many SAP CC deployments serve multiple clients, each operating as a separate logical tenant within a single system. In such environments, a single user, for example, a billing specialist managing both retail and wholesale clients, previously needed two separate user accounts, one for each client. Similarly, a user requiring both business and administrator roles within the same system could not previously manage these roles through a single user account. Such requirements often resulted in duplicate user accounts and additional administrative overhead, making access control difficult to manage and maintain consistently. 
 The current release addresses these challenges by fundamentally reworking the user account model. A single user identity can now hold independent role assignments at the system level and across multiple clients simultaneously. 
 The Manage User Accounts and Manage Permissions Cockpit apps have also been updated to display and manage all role assignments for a user across different contexts from a single screen. 
 When a user has assignments in more than one context, a context selection page is displayed in the Cockpit, while a dialog appears in the Core Tool during login. The user can simply select the context they want to work on for that session. 

 [Figure 2: Reworked Manage User Accounts app showing multi-client assignment] 

 [Figure 3: Context selection page in Cockpit] 

 [Figure 4: Context selection dialog at login in Core Tool] 
 The new model also brings full SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS) integration: the SCIM API has been redesigned with flat endpoints and stable group identifiers, allowing CIS to provision users across all client contexts automatically. A new OAuth2 token endpoint supports machine-to-machine authentication for service users. 
 Benefits: 
 One user identity across the entire SAP CC system - eliminates duplicate accounts in multi-client deployments 
 No need for duplicate user accounts in case of users having multiple roles (business and administrator) in the same system. 
 Enables SAP Cloud Identity Services integration for automated user provisioning across all client contexts 
 For more information: What's New: Multiple Assignments for Individual User Accounts and Effects on User Interfaces 
 Client Copy Procedure 
 When setting up a new client, whether for migrating to a new SAP CC system, onboarding a new business unit, or consolidating existing landscapes often requires recreating the entire configuration from scratch which are typically time-consuming and error prone. 
 For instance, administrators may need to replicate pricing models, and other client-specific settings while ensuring consistency between the source and target systems. Manually recreating these configurations across systems increases administrative effort and the risk of inconsistencies or human errors. 
 With this release, SAP CC introduces a client copy capability in the Setup Tool CLI, simplifying this process. System administrators can export the complete configuration of a source client into a self-contained XML archive, transform JCo destinations to point to the target system, and import the archive into a target client, either within the same system or on a different one. 
 New Setup Tool commands are available to support each step of the process: export, clean, and import. This capability complements the system-level CSV-based copy functionality introduced in FPS1, providing administrators with configuration copy capabilities at both the system and client levels . 
 PS: Note that both the source and target systems must be down during the procedure . 
 Benefits: 
 System administrators can replicate client configurations between systems using a single CLI command sequence 
 XML-based transport is self-contained and portable — suitable for cross-system migrations and environment refreshes 
 Complements the existing system-level CSV copy, giving administrators granular control at both system and client scope 
 For more information: Client Copy & Multiclient System Copy 
 Other Enhancements 
 Response Item Definition in Manage Rate Plans 
 While calculating usage charges or rating subscription services, calling applications often need more than just the calculated fee. For example, a logistics company's bid management application may need additional pricing details to prepare a customer quotation, similarly, an e-commerce application may need pricing information to display charges as items are added to a shopping cart. 
 Response Items enable SAP CC to return configurable fields to the calling application as part of the runtime response. Unlike charged items, which drive financial transactions and billing records, response items provide additional informational feedback without creating billing records. 
 Until FPS2, Response Items could only be configured at the charge plan level using the Core Tool. With FPS2, pricing specialists can now configure Response Items directly in the Cockpit through a dedicated Response Item Definition page in the Manage Rate Plans Fiori app. The page is accessible for each charge within a rate plan, allowing specialists to define and maintain the fields and their values that should be returned to the calling application when the rate plan is used for rating or charging. 
 This enhancement simplifies response item configuration and is fully aligned with the new RESTful Rating Service introduced in FPS2. 

 [Figure 5: New Response Item Definition page in the Manage Rate Plans app] 
 Benefits: 
 Pricing specialists can configure response item definitions directly in the Cockpit 
 Enables the new RESTful Rating Service to return response items to the caller for rate plans 
 Full Cockpit UI support with field-level editing, synchronization, and discard operations 
 For more information: Configuration of Response Item Definitions in Cockpit (New) 
 Response Items in SOAP Web Services 
 Enterprise applications often rely on SOAP-based integrations to communicate with SAP CC for charging and recharging operations. In these scenarios, calling applications may need additional pricing information alongside the calculated fees to support downstream processing and business decisions. 
 With FPS2, SAP CC extends Response Item support to SOAP Charging and Recharging web services , enabling structured pricing information to be returned alongside the calculated fees. This is supported through two new SOAP service versions: Charging v2 (/v2/chargeableItemCharging) and Recharging v3 (/v3/recharging). 
 This enhancement brings the same structured response capability to SOAP-based integrations, allowing external applications to receive additional configured response fields along with charging and recharging results. 

 Additional Improvements 
 HTTP/2 support for Cockpit and Core Server REST/SOAP APIs — HTTP/1.1 clients continue to work without configuration changes 
 Support for SLES 16 — SAP CC 2025 FPS2 is certified on SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16 
 Support for AIX (rs6000_64) — new installer data units available for IBM AIX on Power PC 64-bit 
 Support for IBM PowerPC Little Endian (linuxppc64le) — new installer data units available for IBM Power PC Little Endian 
 Enhancements of SCIM API for bett

items.title: Quick Data Panel and Drag-and-Drop Measure Reordering in 2026 Q4 QRC
items.author: GregBotticchio
items.text:
Building a table in SAP Analytics Cloud has always involved two distinct challenges: getting the right model objects onto the right axes quickly, and arranging them in the order that makes your analysis readable. Both tasks required indirect workarounds, navigating away from the builder to find objects, or relying on Sort settings as a substitute for true layout control. 
 With the 2026 Q4 QRC , SAP Analytics Cloud addresses both in the same release. A new Quick Data Panel brings model objects directly into the Quick Builder so analysts can place them with a single drag, at view time. And for report designers working with SAP Business Warehouse data, drag-and-drop reordering of measures and calculations is now available directly in the Builder and Quick Builder panels. 
 Together, these two features make the table authoring experience more direct, more fluid, and more in your control. 

 Quick Data Panel in the Quick Builder 
 When building a table or chart in the Quick Builder, there was no direct way to see all model objects from within the panel, adding a dimension or measure meant navigating away, with no guarantee of precise axis placement on return. 
 A Data Panel Built Into the Quick Builder 
 The Quick Data Panel presents a clean, purpose-built view of the model: Accounts or Measures members from the primary structure dimension, all model dimensions, and a search box to locate any object instantly. Options to add new models, create calculations, or add input controls are deliberately excluded , keeping the focus on objects that are ready to be placed in the widget. 

 [SCREENSHOT: Quick Builder panel open alongside a table widget, showing the integrated Data Panel with Accounts/Measures members and model dimensions listed, and the search box at the top] 
 Drag and Drop Directly onto Axes 
 Analysts can drag any dimension or measure from the Quick Data Panel and drop it directly onto a table or chart axis, rows, or columns, at the exact position intended. The widget updates immediately, with no intermediate steps and no repositioning required after the fact. 
 Existing Objects Remain Accessible 
 Calculations, Input Controls, Cross Calculations, and Calculated Dimensions are hidden by default to keep the panel clean. If any of these already exist within the widget, their sections remain visible, so analysts working with established widgets find everything exactly where they expect it. 

 Drag-and-Drop Measure Reordering for SAP Business Warehouse Tables 
 For report designers working with live SAP Business Warehouse data, the order in which measures and calculations appear in a table shapes how readers interpret results. Yet until now, that order was largely outside the designer's direct control. 
 Drag and Drop to Reorder Measures and Calculations 
 Designers can now drag measures, accounts, and calculations within the Measure Structure in the Builder panel to define their preferred display order. Changes take effect immediately in both the Builder panel and the table widget, provided the table's sort setting is set to "Default". Visual feedback throughout the drag operation highlights valid drop positions and blocks invalid ones, making the interaction predictable and preventing accidental misplacement. 

 [SCREENSHOT: Builder panel showing a measure being dragged to a new position within the Measure Structure, with visual indicators highlighting valid drop zones] 
 Adding Members from the Data Panel 
 Designers can also drag measures, accounts, and calculations from the Data Panel and drop them into any valid position within the Measure Structure, at the top, between existing members, or at the bottom, in a single gesture. 
 ⚠️ Input Controls are an exception: they can only be placed at the end of the structure, are always displayed last in the table widget, and are not draggable. Nothing can be dropped after the last Input Control in the list. 
 How the Designer-Defined Order Is Saved 
 Any order established via drag and drop is saved as the new " Default order " for the story and table widget, replacing the backend default. It persists across saves and reloads. The table reflects this order when its sort is set to "Default"; a table-level sort (A to Z, Z to A, or custom) takes precedence without overwriting the Builder panel order. (Note: synchronisation in this release is mono-directional : Builder panel changes update the table, but not vice versa.) 
 Client Calculations Follow Their Anchor Member 
 When a member with an associated Client Calculation is reordered, the Client Calculation moves with it automatically, preserving the logical relationship between the base member and its derived calculation without any extra steps. 

 Why This Matters 
 Placement and layout are both part of analysis. The Quick Data Panel eliminates the last significant navigation detour in the Quick Builder, model objects are now visible and placeable in a single gesture. Drag-and-drop measure reordering gives SAP Business Warehouse report designers the direct layout control they previously had to approximate with Sort settings. 
 Together, these two features move table authoring in SAP Analytics Cloud closer to the fluent, direct-manipulation experience analysts and designers expect. We encourage you to explore both capabilities in the 2026 Q4 QRC and share your feedback.

I'm Charis from the CX Solution & Product Learning team, and I am excited to announce that our course Creating and Configuring Web Content for SAP Commerce Cloud has been updated and is now available on learning.sap.com ! 
 🌟 About This Course 
 SAP Commerce Cloud gives business users powerful tools to manage and personalize storefront content — without needing to write a single line of code. This course covers everything a web content manager needs to work confidently with the platform: from understanding the theoretical foundations of the Web Content Management System (WCMS) and the WCMS Page Model, to performing everyday tasks in SmartEdit such as creating pages, managing navigation, applying restrictions, and delivering personalized customer experiences. 
 ❓ What's New in This Update 
 This update focuses on making the course more accessible and up to date. Here is a summary of the key changes: 
 Reduced and simplified text throughout the course, with a particular focus on more complex topics such as the WCMS Page Model, to make concepts easier to follow. 
 New features relevant to a general introduction to WCMS in SAP Commerce Cloud have been added to reflect the latest platform capabilities. 
 Simplified lesson assessments with fewer, more focused questions to keep knowledge checks concise and relevant. 
 New content on Intelligent Selling Services , including demo videos, to introduce learners to personalization-driven commerce capabilities. 
 📝 Course Details 
 Level Beginner 
 Duration 3 hr 27 min 
 Units 4 
 Achievement Leads to Achievement 
 Access Free on learning.sap.com 
 🎓 Learning Objectives 
 By the end of this course, you will be able to: 
 Break down the theoretical foundation for web content management in SAP Commerce Cloud, including the WCMS architecture and Page Model 
 Perform basic tasks in SmartEdit such as previewing pages, adding and exchanging CMS components, managing navigation, and working with workflows 
 Use SmartEdit's Advanced Edit mode for more complex content management tasks, including shared components and version snapshots 
 Apply personalization options to optimize the customer experience on the storefront using target groups and commerce customizations 
 📚 What's Inside? 
 Unit 1 — Analyzing the Theory of SAP Commerce Cloud Web Content Management A solid grounding in the concepts behind the WCMS module — covering its architecture, the WCMS Page Model, and how templates, content slots, and CMS components relate to one another. 
 Unit 2 — Learning the Foundation of Being a Web Content Manager Get hands-on with SmartEdit. This unit takes you through the core day-to-day tasks: previewing and editing pages, synchronising content, handling restrictions, working with shared components, assembling version snapshots, managing storefront navigation, and collaborating through workflows. 
 Unit 3 — Improving Your Web Content Manager Skills via SmartEdit's Advanced Edit Mode Go beyond the basics with SmartEdit's Advanced Edit mode, extending your ability to handle more complex content management scenarios with greater control. 
 Unit 4 — Optimizing CX on the Storefront by Using Personalization Options Discover how to personalise the storefront experience for different customer segments — including setting up commerce customisations that trigger search profiles and promotions, and exploring additional personalisation approaches. 
 👥 Who Is This For? 
 This course is designed for business users responsible for web content management on SAP Commerce Cloud storefronts — content editors, web content managers, and anyone involved in managing and publishing storefront pages. No technical background is required. 
 🏅 Earn a Knowledge Badge 
 Course completion rewards learners with a digital knowledge badge, demonstrating their skills in SAP Commerce Cloud customer support and order management—perfect for sharing achievements both internally and on professional networks.

 You can find the updated course here: Creating and Configuring Web Content for SAP Commerce Cloud 
 We hope you enjoy the updated content! If you have any questions or feedback, feel free to share them in the comments below.

Premikati achieved a 17% conversion rate from engaged contacts to warm leads and now treats the SAP Partner Demand Center as a continuous campaign engine. It's a model any partner can follow.

items.title: Enterprise Landscape Transformation: Moving Beyond Application Consolidation
items.author: Sneka_E
items.text:
Introduction 
 As enterprises grow across geographies, business units, and operational functions, their IT landscapes naturally become more complex. 
 Over the years, organizations introduce applications to address specific business requirements, support new operations, comply with regional regulations, and improve operational efficiency. Acquisitions, business expansions, technology upgrades, and individual transformation initiatives further contribute to this growth. 
 Although each application may have been introduced to solve a particular problem, the cumulative result can be a highly diversified IT landscape consisting of multiple platforms, overlapping functionalities, disconnected systems, legacy technologies, and complex integration dependencies. 
 This creates an important question for enterprise leadership: 
 Does the existing application landscape continue to support the organization's long-term business and technology strategy, or has it become a constraint to transformation? 
 This is where Enterprise Architecture and application rationalization become important. 
 A unified enterprise landscape is not necessarily about operating every business function through a single application. It is about establishing a well-governed, integrated, and strategically aligned ecosystem in which applications have clearly defined responsibilities and collectively support enterprise objectives. 
 Why Do Large Enterprises Have Diversified IT Landscapes? 
 A diversified application landscape rarely develops overnight. It is usually the result of several years of business growth and technology decisions. 
 Some of the common contributing factors include: 
 1. Business Expansion and Geographical Diversity 
 Organizations operating across multiple countries and business units often introduce different applications to address local operational requirements, regulatory obligations, and regional business processes. 
 2. Mergers and Acquisitions 
 When organizations acquire other businesses, they often inherit different ERP systems, applications, databases, and technology platforms. Integrating these environments can be complex, resulting in multiple systems performing similar business functions. 
 3. Independent Technology Decisions 
 Different departments may independently select applications based on immediate business requirements without considering the organization's overall enterprise architecture strategy. 
 4. Legacy System Dependencies 
 Applications that have been operational for many years may continue to support critical business processes. Even when modern alternatives are available, replacing these applications can be difficult because of integrations, historical data, custom developments, and operational dependencies. 
 5. Functional Overlaps 
 Different applications may provide similar capabilities across departments or business units. For example, an enterprise may operate multiple document management systems, reporting platforms, workflow tools, or procurement applications. 
 6. Department-Specific Solutions and Shadow IT 
 Business teams may introduce independent solutions to address operational gaps. Over time, these applications become part of the enterprise landscape, sometimes without sufficient architectural governance. 
 The result is not simply a large number of applications. It is a landscape where visibility, ownership, integration, governance, and cost management become increasingly challenging. 
 Why Are Enterprises Now Looking Towards a Unified Landscape? 
 Application unification and rationalization are increasingly important because organizations are looking beyond individual application performance and evaluating the efficiency of their overall technology ecosystem. 
 Several business and technology drivers are influencing this shift. 
 Key Driver Enterprise challenge Expected outcome 
 Cost optimization Multiple licenses, infrastructure, maintenance, and support costs Optimized IT expenditure 
 Operational efficiency Similar applications supporting overlapping processes Standardized operations 
 Data consistency Data distributed across disconnected platforms Improved data governance 
 Integration complexity Multiple point-to-point interfaces Simplified integration architecture 
 Security and compliance Different security controls and technology standards Consistent governance 
 Technology modernization Aging platforms and unsupported technologies Modern and sustainable architecture 
 Scalability Difficulty supporting business expansion Flexible and scalable landscape 
 AI and digital transformation Fragmented data and disconnected business context Better foundation for enterprise-wide innovation 
 The emergence of cloud platforms, enterprise data platforms, automation, and Business AI further increases the importance of a well-structured application landscape. 
 For example, implementing AI capabilities across an enterprise requires more than deploying an AI solution. Organizations also need reliable data, defined business processes, controlled access, and integration with relevant enterprise systems. 
 Therefore, landscape unification is increasingly becoming an enabler for broader digital transformation. 
 The Enterprise Architect's Role in Landscape Rationalization 
 An Enterprise Architect plays a central role in understanding the current IT environment and defining how it should evolve. 
 The objective is to connect business strategy with application, data, technology, and integration architecture. 
 Rather than evaluating applications independently, the Enterprise Architect considers the complete ecosystem. 
 This includes understanding: 

 Which business capabilities are supported by each application? 

 Which departments and geographical entities use the application? 

 Are multiple applications supporting the same business capability? 

 What are the upstream and downstream dependencies? 

 What is the application's business criticality? 

 Does the application align with the organization's technology strategy? 

 What would be the business impact of replacing or retiring it? 
 This requires a structured assessment rather than decisions based solely on application age, licensing costs, or the number of users. 
 An important foundation is an accurate application inventory, supported by application ownership, business capability mapping, technology information, and dependency relationships. 
 Enterprise Architecture platforms such as SAP LeanIX can help establish this transparency and support application portfolio assessment and rationalization. 
 Key Evaluation Criteria for Application Rationalization 
 One of the most important steps in rationalization is defining a consistent set of evaluation parameters. 
 Every application should be assessed from both business and technical perspectives. 
 The following criteria provide a practical assessment model. 
 A. Business and Functional Assessment 
 Evaluation parameter What should be evaluated? 
 Business Criticality How important is the application to business operations? 
 Functional Fit How effectively does the application support the required business processes? 
 Business Capability Alignment Which business capabilities does the application support? 
 Functional Overlap Are similar capabilities available in other enterprise applications? 
 User Adoption How extensively is the application used across the organization? 
 Geographical Coverage Does it support multiple countries, regions, and business units? 
 Business Value What measurable business value does the application deliver? 
 B. Technical and Architecture Assessment 
 Evaluation parameter What should be evaluated? 
 Technical Fit Does the technology align with enterprise architecture standards? 
 Technology Lifecycle Is the application based on supported and maintained technology? 
 Integration Complexity How many integrations and dependencies does it have? 
 Scalability Can it support future business and transaction growth? 
 Performance and Availability Does it meet operational performance and availability requirements? 
 Architecture Alignment Does it align with the target technology and integration architecture? 
 Technical Debt Are there significant customizations, obsolete components, or maintenance challenges? 
 C. Financial Assessment 
 Evaluation parameter What should be evaluated? 
 Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) What is the overall cost of operating the application? 
 Licensing Cost What are the recurring software and subscription costs? 
 Infrastructure Cost What are the hosting, storage, network, and infrastructure expenses? 
 Maintenance and Support What resources and costs are required for ongoing support? 
 Modernization Cost What investment would be required to upgrade or migrate the application? 
 Consolidation Opportunity What potential savings can be achieved by consolidating overlapping solutions? 
 D. Security, Risk, and Compliance Assessment 
 Evaluation parameter What should be evaluated? 
 Security Posture Does the application meet enterprise security standards? 
 Regulatory Compliance Does it satisfy applicable regional and industry requirements? 
 Data Privacy How does it manage sensitive and business-critical information? 
 Vendor Risk Is the vendor reliable and capable of providing long-term support? 
 Business Continuity Are backup, recovery, and disaster recovery arrangements adequate? 
 Obsolescence Risk Are there unsupported components or end-of-life technologies? 
 E. Strategic and Future Readiness Assessment 
 Evaluation parameter What should be evaluated? 
 Strategic Alignment Does the application support the organization's long-term business strategy? 
 Cloud Readiness Can it support the organization's cloud and hosting strategy? 
 Data Readiness Can its data be governed, integrated, and made available for enterprise analytics? 
 Automation Readiness Can it support process automation and workflow improvements? 
 AI Readiness Can it participate in the organization's future AI-enabled architecture? 
 Future Scalability Can it accommodate new business models, acquisitions, and expansion? 
 These parameters should be adapted to the organization's industry, regulatory environment, transformation priorities, and business requirements. 
 Importantly, not every parameter should carry equal weight. A mission-critical application may justify higher operating costs, while a low-cost application may still be a rationalization candidate if it introduces significant security or technology risks. 
 How Should an Enterprise Conduct a Rationalization Assessment? 
 A structured, phased approach helps enterprises move from understanding their existing landscape to making informed rationalization decisions. 
 Step 1: Establish the Application Inventory 
 Collect the list of applications across business units, departments, geographical locations, and technology environments. 
 Capture relevant information such as application name, description, owner, vendor, hosting environment, technology stack, users, lifecycle status, and business function. 
 Step 2: Map Applications to Business Capabilities 
 Identify which business capabilities and processes are supported by each application. 
 This is particularly important for identifying functional overlaps. 
 For example, if three different applications support document management across three business units, the assessment should determine whether these are genuinely different business requirements or opportunities for consolidation. 
 Step 3: Identify Application Dependencies 
 Document application-to-application integrations, interfaces, data exchanges, infrastructure dependencies, and critical upstream and downstream relationships. 
 An application that appears redundant may still support several critical business processes through integrations. 
 Therefore, dependency analysis must happen before recommending its retirement.

 A legacy outgrows its digital roots 

 For over a decade, SAP had been Oliva’s digital backbone, but the business has evolved dramatically. What was once a single-entity operation has blossomed into a complex, global enterprise with legal entities across the United States, Nicaragua, and Honduras, each with its own currency, tax laws, and compliance rules. 

 “The structural truth today is that Oliva Group isn’t one company anymore,” explained Eduard Bouten, COO, Oliva Group. “Our legacy system was built for smaller, simpler operations. It was a good fit a decade ago, but it was holding us back.” 

 Recognizing an inflection point, the team saw an opportunity. “We wanted to do better, to sell more, to be more efficient, and to use modern tools to help us out,” Bouten noted. The primary goal was clear: transform its data from a simple record into a decisive strategic asset. 

 A modern foundation for a legacy brand 

 Oliva’s search for a new ERP was guided by the need for a system that could master its multi-company complexity while providing a foundation for future growth. It chose SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition because it offered a unified, intelligent platform managed entirely by SAP. 

 “SAP manages the infrastructure, the security, the upgrades,” Bouten said. “This allows our team to focus on our core passion, making exceptional cigars, not running servers.” 

 By adopting the system’s pre-configured best practices, Oliva is transforming its operations. It can now achieve real-time financial consolidation, slashing a three-week reporting lag to provide an instant, unified view across all entities. The new platform bridges the information gap between leadership in Miami and operations on the ground, delivering end-to-end supply chain visibility from raw tobacco to finished goods. This creates a single source of truth to power analytics and drive growth. 

 Building a partnership on trust 

 A project of this magnitude required a partner who could do more than just implement software. For Oliva, the choice of LeverX came down to one crucial element: trust. 

 “In these major projects, there’s always an imbalance of knowledge,” Bouten shared. “You need a partner who listens, understands your way of working, and can bridge what you need with the realities of the system.” 

 LeverX invested eight months in understanding Oliva’s unique business, earning that trust long before a contract was signed. “We believe LeverX is in our corner so we can be successful,” Bouten affirmed. 

 This commitment was echoed by the LeverX team. “Oliva’s story is one of heritage meeting ambition,” said Ken Garcia, senior client partner at LeverX. “Our goal was to be the partner they could trust to build a digital foundation that respects their legacy while fueling their future. With SAP, we’re providing them with the real-time insights and scalability to grow for generations to come.” 

 A foundation for innovation 

 With a solid, clean, and connected data foundation now in place, the conversation at Oliva is already turning to future innovations like business AI. But it’s taking a pragmatic approach, ensuring all stakeholders are confident in the new system first. 

 “Look at it like a pyramid,” Bouten concluded. “The bigger the base, the higher you can go. SAP is that base, which will allow us to peak higher.” 

 By establishing this trusted, unified system, Oliva is setting the groundwork for truly transformative technologies. It’s a testament to a company that understands lasting success—like a perfectly aged cigar—is built layer by layer, with patience, expertise, and an unwavering commitment to quality.

We are pleased to announce that SAP has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud ERP for Product-Centric Enterprises for the fifth year in a row. 

 SAP has been a Leader in this Magic Quadrant every year since its inception in 2022. 

 We believe this recognition, based on our Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute, reflects our commitment to helping product-centric enterprises—from midmarket manufacturers to the most complex global operators—run smarter with integrated, AI-powered cloud ERP. 

 At SAP, this is what our Autonomous Enterprise strategy is designed to deliver.

 When we speak with customers, they tell us that what sets SAP apart isn’t just the depth of our cloud ERP capabilities, it’s how we bring together process intelligence, AI-enabled automation, and deep industry context into a unified platform built for the full product life cycle. Through Joule, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Knowledge Graph, and SAP Signavio, we help product-centric organizations discover inefficiencies, re-engineer processes, and execute AI-enabled operations from design and engineering through planning, manufacturing, and distribution. 

 In practice, that means a connected design-to-operate platform: SAP Integrated Product Development ties engineering BOMs and product structures directly into procurement and production orders, so design changes propagate through the supply chain automatically rather than through manual handoffs. SAP Integrated Business Planning balances demand signals against multi-level bills of material, production capacity, and supplier constraints in real time. SAP Digital Manufacturing brings cloud-native execution and quality management to the shopfloor across both discrete and process industries. And SAP Transportation Management connects outbound logistics back to the same operational record—giving product-centric companies end-to-end visibility from the first component to the last mile. 

 Through SAP Green Ledger, customers can link carbon emissions directly to specific products, production runs, and supplier inputs—enabling audit-ready sustainability reporting that serves both financial compliance and emerging digital product passport requirements. What resonates most is that this isn’t AI layered onto ERP. Our AI runs on the application logic and process models customers already have: Joule Assistants coordinate agents for each role—the production planner responding to a supply disruption, the quality manager escalating a deviation, the logistics coordinator rerouting a shipment—and those agents execute inside the transaction, with approvals, exception handling, and audit trails built in. 

 When we speak with manufacturers, the AI they ask about is the AI on the plan and the plant floor. To illustrate just a few of the business value outcomes, the Supply Chain Planning Assistant turns an alert into a decision: its agents analyze the root cause of a plan exception, recommend the resolution for the planner to approve, and build service-versus-inventory curves so inventory targets are set against capital rather than in a spreadsheet, designed to cut excess and obsolete inventory by 20% and lift order fill rate by 15%. 

 The Manufacturing Assistant detects a line disruption as it emerges, realigns the production schedule to live floor conditions, and flags material shortages with alternative components, designed to cut scrap and defect rates by 24% and raise production supervisor productivity by 19%. 

 For us, recognition as a Leader is a milestone, not the end of the journey. Customers tell us they want to run their largest global operations in the public cloud, commercial terms that stay simple as they grow, and the Autonomous Enterprise in production rather than on a road map.  Autonomous Enterprise in production: General availability for autonomous enterprise agents, Joule Work, and Joule Studio is now underway in a phased rollout, expanding SAP’s robust AI portfolio. Joule already runs in production at hundreds of customers, governed across their life cycle by SAP AI Agent Hub, and SAP’s own 110,000 employees run on it, with a 20% productivity gain in finance, HR, and procurement. The latest capabilities can be found on SAP Discovery Center . 

 Looking ahead, we remain focused on a cloud ERP foundation built for the complexity of product-centric industries, AI that operates with the trust and governance businesses require, and the flexibility to scale from the midmarket to the most complex global manufacturers.

items.title: From Prototypes to Outcomes: What AgenticAI Summit Revealed and Where SAP Has Been A Front Runner
items.author: anuj_gupta_octo
items.text:
Thought leadership — Part 1 of 2 | Author: Anuj Gupta, Office of the CTO, SAP Platform context: This post references capabilities in SAP Business AI Platform, SAP BTP (Business Technology Platform), SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP AI Agent Hub, Joule Studio, and SAP Knowledge Graph — available as part of SAP's AI portfolio. 
 There has been a shift in Enterprise AI this year — from prototypes to real agent outcomes. The question is no longer whether AI agents can do impressive things in demos — they can. The question is whether they can be trusted to do those things reliably, safely, and at scale in production. Frontier models have advanced to the point where agents can handle complex, multi-step business tasks autonomously. Capturing that capability at enterprise scale requires a new platform paradigm. We had a similar shift for services when Microservices architecture became a preferred approach over Service Oriented Architecture. I see this as another shift where distributed systems now have reasoning and self-improving capabilities — and the opportunity is to make that power reliable, safe, trustworthy, and transparent. 
 After two days at the Agentic AI Summit at UC Berkeley this July, it was much clearer. The summit brought together the teams that have shipped agents at enterprise scale, and the conversation was almost entirely about what it takes to build a reliable, scalable, and trustworthy platform: identity, governance, evaluation, runtime safety, and the orchestration that holds it all together. 
 SAP's AI-native North Star architecture frames the destination precisely: a shift from software as a service to outcome as a service — where AI agents, grounded in deep business context, execute across enterprise boundaries and continuously learn from results. Powerful models make this possible. An enterprise-grade platform — trusted, observable, governable, and connected to the data and processes that make outcomes real — is what makes it repeatable. 
 What the summit confirmed is that the industry is converging on exactly the platform SAP has been building toward. This post is about what that convergence looks like — and what SAP has already been building. 
 What the summit made clear 
 The conversation at Berkeley had a consistent shape across every session. Teams that have shipped agents at enterprise scale — OpenAI, Anthropic, Scale AI, Meta AI — were talking about what it takes to make agents reliable, safe, and continuously improving once they're in production. 
 METR's research on measuring AI ability to complete long software tasks captured the trajectory: two years ago, frontier models could reliably complete tasks measured in seconds; today, they handle multi-hour software engineering tasks — with task duration doubling roughly every seven months. 
 Peter Steinberger, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI and head of the OpenClaw project, described running 60+ collaborating sub-agents in production — generating pull requests and deploying code continuously. The majority of the engineering effort was on agent hand-off architecture and context continuity, not on the underlying model. Across sessions, a consistent message emerged: workload identity and runtime governance aren't optional extras — they're the precondition for any agent operating reliably at enterprise scale. 
 The pattern is consistent: frontier model capabilities have unlocked a new class of enterprise automation. The platform around those models — identity, governance, evaluation, runtime safety — is what converts that capability into reliable, trustworthy production outcomes. 
 The trends the industry is converging on 
 Here are the shifts that dominated every session and every hallway conversation at the summit. Each one represents an area where the industry has moved from experimentation to engineering discipline. 
 1. Agent identity is becoming foundational infrastructure 
 When a software agent accesses your financial systems, submits a procurement request, or triggers a business workflow, you need to answer: which agent did this, on whose behalf, and under what authorization? Traditional identity systems were designed for humans. They weren't built for autonomous agents making hundreds of API calls per minute across dozens of systems. 
 The industry's answer is workload identity : short-lived cryptographic credentials, automatically rotated, scoped to a specific purpose, tied to a known agent registration. IBM Research demonstrated this at the summit using SPIFFE/SPIRE-based architecture — the key design principle being that an agent must never inherit more authority than was explicitly delegated, at every handoff in the chain. 
 Traditional IAM was designed for static, pre-provisioned access: a human admin defines roles and permission groups ahead of time, and the system assumes everything was anticipated. Autonomous agents break this model. An agent's authorization needs are determined at runtime — shaped by the task it is executing, the context it is operating in, and the scope it was explicitly delegated for that specific action. When something goes wrong, accountability requires answering: which agent did this, under what authorization, on whose behalf — and that chain must be reconstructable from runtime identity, not inferred from a pre-configured role. 
 2. Runtime safety is replacing prompt guardrails 
 Prompt-level filtering was the 2024 approach to AI safety. Today, the leading teams have moved to a different approach: policy enforcement integrated directly into the agent execution layer. Not content filtering — runtime governance . Continuous monitoring, automated red teaming built into the release pipeline, sandboxed tool execution, and governance pipelines that intervene when an agent's behavior deviates from its declared purpose. 
 The framing that came up repeatedly: safety is an engineering discipline, not a content moderation problem. Dawn Song's research lab at Berkeley alone has six active projects in this space, with commercial work covering automated red teaming and runtime policy enforcement. 
 A concrete signal of where this is heading: AWS researchers recently released Dogwood, an open-source runtime verification language for AI agents. The key insight Dogwood addresses is that traditional authorization systems like Cedar are point-in-time — they can evaluate whether a single request is permitted, but they cannot enforce rules about sequences of actions over time. Dogwood introduces temporal policies : governance rules that evaluate an agent's full execution history, enabling constraints like requiring approval before a specific action, enforcing correct tool-call ordering, rate-limiting tool usage within a time window, or blocking actions after certain prior events. This is precisely the kind of runtime governance the industry is converging on — policies that understand not just what an agent is asking to do, but what it has already done. 
 3. Evaluation is becoming the operating system for autonomous agents 
 Most teams evaluate before release — test cases, benchmarks, human reviewers. The summit's clearest message: pre-release validation is necessary but not sufficient. Production behavior diverges from offline benchmarks, and the divergence grows over time. 
 The leading organizations now evaluate at multiple levels simultaneously: business outcomes, task success rates, component quality (planning, retrieval, memory, tool use), and continuous diagnostics. Michele Catasta from Replit talked about the target state: production telemetry driving hypothesis generation, automated fixes, validation, and re-deployment in a closed loop. Scale AI's Priya Ponnapalli reframed the business case directly — human oversight is the operating cost of AI. Evaluation investment reduces that cost. The teams that skip continuous evaluation aren't saving on engineering; they're paying for it indefinitely in human oversight that never gets reduced. 
 4. Autonomy is earned progressively — and can be stepped back 
 As agent capability expands — tasks that once took seconds now run for hours, with week-long autonomous execution on the near horizon — the question of how much autonomy to grant has become more consequential than ever. 
 The answer that emerged consistently across every enterprise deployment story at the summit: nobody ships full autonomy on day one. The pattern is a supervision ladder — agents start under heavy human review, move to confidence-gated execution as reliability is demonstrated, then to exception-based oversight, and eventually to near-full autonomy. As model capability expands, the engineering challenge shifts to the runtime infrastructure that makes long-running execution safe: durable execution, checkpointing, graceful recovery, human approval gates, and orchestration that can sustain agent work across interruptions and multi-step processes. 
 This isn't just a deployment pattern — it's a value realization pattern. Each rung represents a reduction in human oversight cost. The teams that define the ladder explicitly, set the confidence thresholds that gate transitions, and connect evaluation metrics to progression are the ones capturing measurable ROI from their AI investments. 
 Critically, the ladder runs in both directions. If an agent's confidence scores drop, error rates climb, or behavior drifts outside expected bounds, the system should automatically step supervision back up — returning to tighter review until reliability is re-established. Autonomy isn't a promotion that vests permanently; it's a continuous calibration driven by live performance data. The organizations getting this right treat supervision level as a dynamic variable, not a deployment setting. 
 5. Token efficiency is an economic constraint, not an engineering detail 
 A joint poster from multiple leading universities and AI companies documented what practitioners already suspected: agentic workflows consume significantly more tokens than traditional chat — in some cases an order of magnitude more. At enterprise scale, token consumption is a line item on a P&L. It needs to be managed with the same rigor as compute or storage. 
 The leading teams are optimizing across semantic routing, inference routing, context compression, planning efficiency, and cost prediction before execution begins. Intelligent routing — directing tasks to the cheapest model that can reliably complete them — is becoming a standard platform capability, not a custom engineering project. An industry consortium bringing together enterprises and AI companies to advance token economics standards is a signal that this is maturing into an engineering discipline with shared frameworks. Organizations that treat token efficiency as a first-class architectural concern now will have a structural cost advantage as agentic workloads scale. 
 6. The agent platform is the new software factory 
 Multiple teams at the summit presented variations of the same architecture: a standardized platform integrating orchestration, identity, governance, observability, evaluation, deployment, and runtime management. A software factory for AI agents — the same concept that transformed continuous delivery for traditional software, now applied to agentic AI. 
 The teams winning enterprise deployments are competing on the quality of this surrounding platform: the governance, reusable workflows, enterprise integrations, and trust infrastructure that make powerful agents reliable enough to hand real business decisions to. For enterprise buyers, the question has shifted from "how capable is your model?" to "how complete and trustworthy is your platform?" 
 7. Agentic evaluation is replacing static LLM judges as a way to scale 
 Meta AI's Agent-as-a-Judge research was one of the summit's most practically important findings. Evaluator agents are replacing static LLM-based judges, with the ability to assess planning quality, reasoning chains, tool usage

items.title: ASUG Tech Connect 2026 – All Roads Lead to SAP AI
items.author: PeterSpielvogel
items.text:
ASUG Tech Connect 2026 was the best one yet. The combination of many customers, lots of interesting sessions, a convenient, central location in Fort Worth, Texas, and the usual attention to detail by the ASUG team made for a great event. The focus of the event, across keynotes, lectures, hands-on sessions, and the show floor was AI. I appreciated the focus on demonstrating the business value of AI, rather than purely focusing on the technology. 

 The best part of ASUG Tech Connect is the opportunity to connect with customers to understand their priorities for adopting the latest UX and AI innovations. It’s always interesting to see where they are, where they want to go, and the gaps between SAP’s keynote content and the reality in the installed base. This happens during sessions, at meals, and in the expert 1:1 meetings that ASUG schedules for anyone who is interested. I’ll share some of the top issues I encountered across all of these touch points. 
 How do I move from SAP GUI to SAP Fiori? 
 Hard to believe this conversation is still happening, but several customer meetings focused on this topic. One person from a technology company shared his new strategy. 
 “At this point, my leadership team doesn’t care about Fiori, but they do care about Joule. So, my plan is to set the timeline for delivering Joule, and embed Fiori apps into that plan.” 
 Another key enabler is a strong change management program to give people information about what to expect, guide people on how to use the new apps, and provide ongoing opportunities to ask questions. This process often takes 6-24 months, so please don’t expect a quick pivot. Some companies do flip a switch, but it often causes confusion and disruption. 
 Here's are two excellent courses on SAP Fiori: 
 https://learning.sap.com/courses/how-to-deliver-a-great-user-experience-with-sap-s-4hana 
 https://learning.sap.com/courses/learning-the-basics-of-sap-fiori 
 When will AI-assisted features be available for on-prem customers? 
 In my session, “ Embedded AI in SAP Cloud ERP boosts productivity through a better UX ”, I demoed some of the labor-saving features we have included in SAP S/4HANA Cloud that allow users to find, enter, and share data more quickly and easily. As with every presentation of AI capabilities, the question about on-prem arose. Everything I discussed is available today for public cloud, it’s available or on the roadmap for private cloud, and we have no plans to make it available for on-prem customers. Moving to the cloud gives you more agility to adopt the innovations that SAP provides. 
 You can view the slides from my talk here . 

 Peter Spielvogel talking about common issues we hear from customers about usability. 
 How to migrate from SAP Enterprise Portal to SAP Work Zone or whatever is next 
 I did not have much to contribute to this conversation, but fortunate to have my colleague Florian Büch available to take the lead on the topic. He pointed to three excellent resources, two from SAP and one from a partner. 
 Learn how to transition from SAP Enterprise Portal to SAP Build Work Zone 
 The path from SAP Enterprise Portal to SAP Work Zone 
 Establish a central entry point with SAP Build Work Zone 
 How to migrate Web Dynpro Java apps to ABAP? 
 There is no automated tool or migration path to do this. However, this seems like a task that could be well-suited to AI, assuming you have lots of grounding documentation including a specification of what your current app does, the underlying data structures and relationships, and the business logic. While AI can probably give you a reasonable first draft, I would recommend allocating lots of time for testing at all levels – unit, integration, system, and functional testing. AI can do some of the testing, but you will need human involvement to ensure high confidence in your results. 
 Which SAP Fiori apps can I extend or adapt? 
 You can see all the available SAP Fiori apps in the SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library . By applying the appropriate filters, you can see the apps that are available to your S/4HANA version. Each app tells you if or how you can extend it. Find this information in the configuration tab. 

 There is extensive documentation on how to extend SAP Fiori apps in the help portal . 
 What’s the best way to build SAP Fiori apps today? 
 The modern way to build SAP Fiori apps using MCP servers. The documentation discusses developing an app with the MCP Server for SAP Fiori and skills using AI . If you prefer to learn by doing, there is an exercise on the learning.sap.com platform: “ Using MCP Servers for AI-Assisted SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 Development ” 
 Should I use RAP or CAP for my SAP Fiori apps? 
 The SAP Learning platform has a primer that explains the relative merits of ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) and Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) and some tips on when to use which . 
 What is the best way to embrace clean core? 
 The first thing is to understand what clean core is and is not. We have a clean core guide that explains this. As you would expect, we have a lesson on clean core in the SAP Learning platform . 
 Can I use AI-based development tools to create apps for my on-prem system? 
 Yes. You can use Joule Studio or other AI-assisted development tools to create apps for your cloud-based or on-prem system. If you want to try the latest tooling for building SAP Fiori apps, you can try the hands-on exercises from TechEd, although you will need to do this in your own environment. 
 From SAP Fiori elements to agent to Joule Work: The full stack, hands-on: https://github.com/SAP-samples/teched2026-JW163 
 OData to outcomes — Build AI-enabled SAP Fiori apps using SAP Fiori elements https://github.com/SAP-samples/teched2026-JW262 
 Can I build SAP Fiori apps and then transport them to a secure air-gapped environment? 
 This is relevant for many high-security companies, including most in the aerospace and defense industries. Yes, using ABAP and Fiori MCP servers it is possible to create and maintain Fiori applications and later transport them in an air-gapped environment. We recommend you start with the recent tutorial that covers state-of-the-art full stack development of SAP Fiori elements application using RAP. 
 https://github.com/SAP-samples/fiori-abap-fullstack-ai-tutorial 
 More Awards 
 ASUG presented many awards at the event, so, in that spirit, here are my personal awards, based on my interest in helping customers obtain better usability in their SAP Cloud ERP system and generating value from new AI capabilities. The categories are content, surprises, and energy. 
 Content commanders 
 Best customer session . ExxonMobil’s Michael Adrian and Lilissa Chao shared the most detailed, organized, and meticulously planned migration to SAP S/4HANA that I have ever seen. They talked about changes to their business model, architectural updates (clean core!), and some recommendations for others to follow. 

 Best customer tip for SAP Fiori adoption . This came from a 1:1 expert talk I had with a high-tech customer. After a decade of not moving to Fiori, he realized that he was not going to gain management support for a push in 2027. But, he knew of the many productivity improvements that the employees would see from moving from SAP GUI to Fiori. So, his plan was to focus on AI and moving to Joule. There is lots of interest in that from senior leadership. Since Fiori is a prerequisite for Joule (Joule uses the same OData services to retrieve the data from the back end to render the screens), he is finally implementing Fiori as a way to enable AI in his organization. Clever! 
 Best surprise prediction on AI . Some of the most interesting conversations happen spontaneously. I had an especially thought-provoking chat with well-known technology industry analyst Josh Greenbaum on the future of AI in enterprise software. With most companies moving quickly to adopt AI as much as they can to drive productivity improvements many companies are looking at the underlying data quality and change management to ensure a rollout that works. Josh’s insight was that governance and security could end up being the big factor that causes everyone to hit the pause button. Imagine a scenario when 100s or 1000s or millions of agents are hitting back-end systems. How would anyone manage all that? What if one rogue agent from a bad actor slipped in and performed an unauthorized action? Companies would definitely take a step back to assess how to figure out how to prevent future problems. If that happens, you heard it first from Josh. 
 Spontaneous surprises 
 Best customer surprise . After working with Betsy Grant online for 10+ years, we finally met in person. 
 Best newcomer to ASUG Tech Connect . Coming off her keynote debut at TechEd Berlin, Emilia Kunst shared her Joule knowledge in some hands-on labs and the expert 1:1 sessions. 

 Emilia at TechEd in Berlin. She brought the magic to ASUG Tech Connect. 
 Best assist . The ASUG 1:1 Q&A sessions are very popular with customers as they give people a chance to speak with SAP experts. Thanks to Florian Busch for jumping in on short notice to join me in a customer expert 1:1 session to cover Enterprise Portal to Work Zone migration topics. You can see the answers to the questions from the session above. 
 Bringing the energy 
 Best energy solo . I had the opportunity to serve on a panel discussion with the amazing transformation leader Kimberly Sharp . At the ASUG Volunteer Meeting, she won the ASUG spirit award and it’s obvious why. She graciously shared her deep knowledge on a career panel discussion as well as with many individuals in the ASUG hub.

items.title: Migrate Your SAP NetWeaver AS Java Custom Applications to the Cloud — Faster Than You Think
items.author: Ani_Koycheva

The calendar is turning faster than many organizations realize. As SAP has made clear, extended support for SAP Business Suite 7 and SAP NetWeaver — including SAP NetWeaver AS Java 7.5 — ends on December 31, 2030 . After that date, the integrated support path customers have relied on for decades will no longer exist. There will be no kernel patches, no security corrections, no database-specific fixes for these environments. 
 For many organizations, the standard SAP applications running on SAP NetWeaver are well understood: upgrade paths exist, roadmaps are published, timelines are set. But there is a second migration challenge that often gets less attention — and that is frequently the harder one. Custom Java applications built directly on the SAP NetWeaver AS Java platform are woven into business-critical processes across industries. These are not off-the-shelf products with a migration wizard. They are bespoke, often decades old, and deeply tied to platform APIs that simply do not exist in the cloud. 
 That challenge now has a purpose-built answer: the SAP NetWeaver Application Migration Assistant .
