items.title: Four ways to use the AI Native Architecture Advisor, from business problem to solution brief
items.author: cassiobinkowski
items.text:
Every AI project starts with the same architecture conversation. Which steps should an agent take on, and which should stay with rules, workflows or people? Which systems does the solution need to read from and act on, and under whose identity? What can be built with what the customer already has, and where is the North Star? Getting that conversation right early saves weeks later. It is also exactly where SAP's new AI Native Architecture Advisor helps. 
 In this blog post, I explain what the Advisor is and how it works, then walk through four scenarios where architects and developers can put it to work. I tested one of them in detail: a dispute-to-credit process that spans SAP S/4HANA on-premise, Salesforce, a logistics partner's portal and SAP BTP. I close with tips for better results and the limits to keep in mind. 
 In short 
 The AI Native Architecture Advisor is an open-source skill that turns a business problem, a process model or an existing design into an initial AI-native solution design, grounded in SAP's own architecture guidance. 
 It runs in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, where it writes a solution brief, a reasoning log and a visual HTML report, and in Joule Work Desktop, where it delivers the brief as Joule cards. 
 Use it to shape new AI use cases, review existing solutions, reimagine multi-stack processes and design reusable partner agents. Treat every result as a draft for an architect to review.

items.title: SAP PaPM Cloud Standard Model - Automate and Manage Data Deletion in Your Models and Processes
items.author: jemimaj
items.text:
Hello, SAP Community members! 
 If you have spent any time modeling in SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Standard Model ( SAP PaPM Cloud SM) , then you may be familiar with the Delete Data from All Functions / Delete Data from Selected Function option which permanently deletes result data from functions. It is simple and reliable, but it is also a manual operation that cannot be incorporated into a process. 
 That raises a natural question for anyone who runs the same model frequently: what if data cleanup could be part of the process itself, running automatically alongside your calculations? What if you could scope a deletion to just one process, or delete the process data behind multiple process instances in a single action? 
 This blog post introduces three additions in SAP PaPM Cloud SM that bring data deletion into the process lifecycle: 
 Deletion Activity , which can be added to a process template in Modeling ; 
 Delete Process Data button in Process Management, which deletes process data across selected instances in a single action; 
 Delete Process Instance button in Process Management , enhanced to include an option to delete associated process data at the same time. 
 Before we look at each one, a few ground rules apply across all three. 

 Before You Begin 
 To understand how these features work, it is helpful to distinguish between two data layers: 
 Model-level data – result data generated by running functions in an environment 
 Process data – result data generated by running execution activities in a process template or process instance 
 All three features apply the same eligibility rules as the existing data deletion action in Modeling : Model tables with  Transport Data  set to Yes (including functions with linked result model tables) are exempt from environment-wide deletion, unless you use Delete Data from Selected Function or apply a process-based deletion to them. 

 Deletion does not apply to SAP HANA-based functions (Model Table HANA, Model View HANA View, and Model View HANA Table). 
 Deletion access is role-dependent: 
 Screen Roles Scope 
 Modeling 
 MODELING 
 MODELING_USER_ALL 
 Run a Deletion Activity from a process template 

 Process Management 
 EXECUTION_MAN_ALL 
 PROCESSES_ALL 
 Run a Deletion Activity in a process instance 
 Use Delete Process Data 
 Use Delete Process Instance 

 EXECUTION_USER_ALL 
 PROCESSES_OWN 
 Run a Deletion Activity in a process instance (when the activity node does not have assigned teams or when user belongs to a Performer team assigned to the node) 
 Process Scheduler PROCESS_SCHEDULER 
 Run a Deletion Activity as part of a scheduled job 
 For more information on the different role templates, see Role Templates in Standard Model on the SAP Help Portal. 

 Meet the Deletion Activity 
 In the Modeling screen, expand Process Templates inside the Calculation Unit Details . Open the palette, then drag and drop a Process Template onto the Process Templates node. With the palette open, the Activity Templates expands to show activity nodes you can add inside the process template, including the Deletion Activity . Drag it onto the process template. 

 While the Input / Output Activity and Execution Activity prompt you to assign a function, a dropdown called Delete Type determines what data gets deleted when the activity runs. 

 Note 
 Like other activity nodes, the Start Date and Due Date are required fields, as indicated by the validation errors in the header. They define when the Deletion Activity is planned to begin and finish. 

 The Three Delete Types 
 The Delete Type dropdown controls the scope of deletion when the activity runs. There are three options to choose from. 

 Delete data from all functions 
 This option provides the broadest scope, deleting the result data of every eligible function in the environment. Like the Delete Data from All Functions button, data deletion does not apply to functions with linked result model table where Transport Data is set to Yes . 
 Tip 
 Use this when you want a clean slate, such as before a new modeling cycle. Its scope doesn’t depend on other activities in a process template, so it can be kept as a standalone node function and it will function the same. Take for example the screenshots below, the second process template (DAD01) with a standalone activity has the same results as the first process template (DAA01). 

 Important 
 This Delete Type operates environment-wide, regardless of which functions are included in the process template. If the template contains only a subset of functions, the Deletion Activity still deletes data from all eligible functions. 
 Note 
 When a function has a linked result model table, the model table’s function ID appears in the application logs. Data is deleted in both function and its linked result model table. 

 Delete Data from Selected Functions 
 This option deletes the result data of only the functions you choose. Selecting it reveals a Functions for Data Deletion field where you specify one or more functions. 
 Note 
 A validation error appears automatically when this option is selected, and the Functions for Data Deletion field is empty. 

 Important 
 This Delete Type also operates environment-wide, regardless of which functions are included in the process template. If the template contains only a subset of functions, the Deletion Activity still deletes data from specified functions. 
 Tip 
 This option can be set up as an opening node of a process chain or run as a standalone node to delete the previous period’s result data before the next cycle. 

 Delete Data from This Process (Default) 
 This option deletes only the process data produced by the execution activities in its own process. It doesn’t touch modeling-level data or data belonging to any other processes. It is the one to reach for when you want to delete only what a specified process produced. 
 Tips 
 Use this option when a process should delete its own data. It can be placed as the closing or final node to delete process data at the end of a run after results are calculated, so each cycle ends clean. For example, in the screenshot below, after generating the results for the execution activity inside process template PRO_P1_, its results are deleted after the Deletion Activity (DAP01) is run but modeling-level data is retained. 

 When viewing the Data Management Screen (DMS) of a function assigned to an execution activity, activate the Show technical fields option in the header toolbar to view the column FS_PER_PROC_ID_ which shows the process to which the data rows belong to. 

 Note 
 If a process has no generated results from execution activities, nothing is deleted with this Delete Type and data belonging to other processes and modeling-level data are not affected. 
 Using Multiple Deletion Activities 
 A process template can contain more than one Deletion Activity , and each node will delete only what its own Delete Type defines. A process chain might start with a Deletion Activity with Delete Type “Delete data from selected functions” that deletes data for specified functions, before running execution activities that repopulate the tables. Then another Deletion Activity with Delete Type “Delete data from this process” can be placed at the end, deleting the generated results from the process execution. 

 Where the Deletion Activity Runs 
 The Deletion Activity is available wherever process templates and their activities run: Modeling , Process Management , and Process Scheduler . Regardless of where the activity runs, the deletion scope remains the same, with one exception. For Delete Type “Delete data from this process” , the scope depends on which processes it applies to. 
 Deletion Activity in Modeling 
 In Modeling , you run the activity directly from the process template. Like the process template (PRO_M1_) configured with multiple deletion activities below, each activity can be directly run. For “Delete data from this process” , data deletion applies at the process template level on execution activities run from the same process template. 

 De letion Activity in Process Management 
 In the Process Management screen, the Deletion Activity appears as an activity node inside a process instance, alongside other activities. It is run in the same way as an Execution Activity and follows the same authorization model. To run it: 
 Select a process instance from the Processes list with Process State “Deployed” . 
 In the combined view with the Gantt diagram, select the Deletion Activity node. 
 Choose Run button in the header tools. 

 For “Delete data from this process”, the run deletes the process data generated at the process instance level from running execution activities in the selected process instances. In the screenshot above, the process instance (PROMD01) is created from the process template (PRO_M1_) in the previous section. When the Deletion Activity (DAP01) runs after both execution activities in the process instance are run, the process data is deleted from the results table of all execution activities. 

 Deletion Activity in Process Scheduler 
 In the Process Scheduler , the Deletion Activity is selectable in the Activities dropdown, alongside execution activities when creating a job. This allows data cleanup operations to run automatically as part of a scheduled job. 
 For a step-by-step process in scheduling a job, see Process Scheduler on the SAP Help Portal. 
 Referencing the same process template (PRO_M1_) in previous sections, a job can be configured with a Deletion Activity to automate data deletion. For Delete Type “Delete data from this process”, d ata from running execution activities within the same job or targeted process instance are deleted. 
 Note 
 Deletion and execution activities can be combined within the same job definition. 

 Regardless of where it is run or its Delete Type , every Deletion Activity run is recorded in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor under the run type “Run” . 

 Deleting Data on Demand in Process Management 
 T he Deletion Activity handles data deletion built into a process template and can be run manually or automatically as part of a process run. For cases where you need to delete multiple data directly after a process has already run, Process Management provides two additional options: the new Delete Process Data button and the enhanced Delete Process Instance button. 
 Important 
 Both buttons are greyed out for users with PROCESSES_OWN or EXECUTION_USER_ALL roles. 
 New: The Delete Process Data Button 
 The Delete Process Data button is found in the Edit section of the Process Management . When you choose the button, it deletes the process data of selected process instances; the same behavior as the Deletion Activit y’s “ Delete data from this process” . Choose this button when you want to delete process results but retain the process instances for rerunning. For example, three process instances have been created from the same process template (PRO_M1) in the screenshot below. Assuming all execution activities in each process instance have been run, when you select process instance PRPD01 and choose Delete Process Data , only the process results associated with PRPD01 are deleted. 

 Before anything is deleted, a confirmation dialog appears: 

 Once you confirm by clicking the Delete Data button, the result is recorded in the message logs on the Process Management screen. 
 Delete Process Data 

 The same logs are available in the Application Monitor and Process Monitor under the run type Delete Process Data . 

 Enhanced: The Delete Process Instance Button 
 The Delete Process Instance button deletes process instances and now, its confirmation dialog includes a checkbox for process data deletion. Previously, deleting an instance left its process data behind. Now, you can delete both in a single step with this button. 

 After confirmation, the result of the action is

items.title: Integrating n8n Workflows with SAP CAP Java: A Hands-on Exploration
items.author: Anjali_Pathak
items.text:
Introduction 
 n8n is an open-source workflow automation platform that enables developers to visually connect applications, APIs, and services to build automated workflows. With its flexible, node-based approach, it simplifies process orchestration while offering the ability to integrate custom logic wherever needed. 
 SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) provides a powerful framework for building enterprise-grade services. The cds-feature-n8n plugin bridges the two by integrating n8n directly into the CAP Java runtime, enabling applications to trigger external workflows in response to entity events without writing custom REST clients or integration handlers. 
 In this blog, we explore a hands-on Proof of Concept (PoC) where a SAP CAP Java service triggers an n8n workflow whenever a new order is created, with the workflow routing orders into different paths based on their status. 
 Prerequisites - Java 21
- Maven 3.6.3+
- Node.js v22.15.0
- n8n running locally via npx n8n 
 Note: The cds-feature-n8n plugin requires CDS 5.2.0 and Spring Boot 4.1.2. Earlier versions will fail at startup. 
 Project Setup 
 Create the project using the SAP CAP CLI: cds init cap-n8n-poc --java 
 Update the root pom.xml with the required versions: <jdk.version>21</jdk.version>
<cds.services.version>5.2.0</cds.services.version>
<spring.boot.version>4.1.2</spring.boot.version> 
 Add the plugin to srv/pom.xml: <dependency>
 <groupId>com.sap.cds</groupId>
 <artifactId>cds-feature-n8n</artifactId>
 <version>0.0.1</version>
</dependency> 
 Data Model 
 Create the entity definition in db/schema.cds : namespace com.example;

entity Orders {
 key ID : UUID;
 customer : String;
 product : String;
 quantity : Integer;
 status : String default 'NEW';
} 
 Service Definition 
 Create the service in srv/orders-service.cds : using { com.example as example } from '../db/schema';

service OrdersService {
 @n8n.process.start: [{ on: 'CREATE', path: 'order-created' }]
 entity Orders as projection on example.Orders;
} 
 The @n8n.process.start annotation is all the integration code you need. It instructs the plugin to trigger the n8n webhook at the order-created path whenever a new Orders entity is created. The plugin takes care of everything else behind the scenes, including event detection, payload extraction, outbox queuing, and webhook delivery - eliminating the need for additional boilerplate code. 
 Configuration 
 Add the following to srv/src/main/resources/application.yaml : spring:
 config.activate.on-profile: default
 sql.init.platform: h2

cds:
 data-source.auto-config.enabled: false
 outbox:
 services:
 N8nOutbox:
 enabled: true

n8n:
 base-url: http://localhost:5678 
 Two things to note here: 
 1. The N8nOutbox outbox service must be explicitly enabled - the plugin looks for a Spring bean qualified with that exact name. 
 2. The n8n.base-url points to your local n8n instance. In production, this would be replaced with the hosted n8n URL. 
 Building the n8n Workflow 
 The workflow consists of three nodes and requires no code . 

 Webhook - Create Order 
 A Webhook node listens for POST requests at /webhook/order-created - the path defined in the @n8n.process.start annotation. Every time an order is created in SAP CAP, the plugin delivers the payload here automatically. 
 Switch - Check Order Status 
 A Switch node in Rules mode routes execution based on the status field: 
 1. Valid Order - status is NEW 
 2. Invalid Order - status is INVALID 
 Downstream Nodes 
 Each branch connects to its own processing node. In this example we keep it simple, but these nodes could send notifications, call external APIs, or invoke AI agents - summarizing orders, classifying them, or triggering intelligent approval workflows - all without touching the SAP CAP Java code. 
 Important: The workflow must be Published before testing. 
 Testing the Integration 
 With the SAP CAP service running and the n8n workflow published, send a POST request to the OData endpoint using Bruno (or any HTTP client). 
 Valid Order: 
 POST http://localhost:8080/odata/v4/OrdersService/Orders

{
 "customer": "Alice",
 "product": "Laptop",
 "status": "NEW"
} 
 Invalid Order: 
 POST http://localhost:8080/odata/v4/OrdersService/Orders

{
 "customer": "Bob",
 "product": "PC",
 "status": "INVALID"
} 
 Within a few seconds, the plugin picks up the event from the outbox and delivers the payload to n8n . Opening the Switch node in n8n confirms the full order payload was received - including the CAP-generated ID, the entity fields, and the webhook URL . 
 Notice the user-agent: Java/21.0.7 header - implies the request originated from the CAP Java runtime. 
 Alice's order with status NEW is routed to the Valid Order branch : 

 Bob's order with status INVALID is routed to the Invalid Order branch : 

 Each branch receives exactly 1 item , correctly routed - confirming the payload was received, evaluated, and processed without any custom Java code. 
 What's Next 
 What we have explored is a practical integration between two powerful platforms , achieved with minimal code and configuration. This is precisely where the cds-feature-n8n plugin adds value: by abstracting the integration complexity , it allows developers to focus on business logic and workflow design rather than building and maintaining custom integration code. 
 The example demonstrated here is just one of many possibilities. The same integration pattern can be extended to a wide range of enterprise use cases: 

 AI-powered workflows: Pass entity data to LLMs through n8n's OpenAI or Anthropic nodes to classify records, generate summaries, identify anomalies, or initiate intelligent approval workflows - all without implementing custom integration logic. 

 Event-driven business processes: Extend the integration to different SAP CAP entities and events , enabling use cases such as invoice processing, customer onboarding, approval workflows, and document generation. 

 Production-ready deployments: Replace the local n8n URL with your hosted n8n instance , configure the required authentication, and leverage the persistent outbox mechanism for reliable webhook delivery and automatic retries. 
 The underlying architecture maintains a clear separation of responsibilities: SAP CAP manages the data model and business logic, while n8n handles workflow orchestration and automation. Together, they provide a flexible approach to extending enterprise applications with event-driven automation and AI capabilities . 
 For more details, refer to the SAP CAP n8n plugin documentation , n8n Workflow Documentation , n8n Integrations & Nodes to learn more about plugin configuration, workflow creation, and available integrations.

items.author: Chaitanya_Sakamuri
items.text:
1. Introduction 
 Starting with SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud 2025 FPS01, tools used during field service activities can now be managed end-to-end across SAP S/4HANA and SAP Field Service and Asset Management (FSA). This integration covers tool master data replication, tool assignment on service orders, reservation and consumption tracking by technicians in the FSA, and confirmation posting back to S/4HANA for billing. 

 # 
 Capability 
 Direction 

 1 
 Master Data Replication 
 S/4HANA → FSA 

 2 
 Tool Replication 
 S/4HANA → FSA 

 3 
 Tool Consumption in FSA 
 In FSA 

 4 
 Confirmation Posting 
 FSA → S/4HANA 

 Figure 1: End-to-end data flow -- Tool Integration between SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA 
 2. Mandatory Requirements 
 Below are the system requirements to use the tools integration. Also the systems should be set up following instructions available at Integration with SAP Field Service and Asset Management | SAP Help Portal 

 System 
 Version 

 SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud 
 2025 FPS01 or higher 

 CPI Package 'SAP S/4HANA Integration with SAP Field Service Management' 
 2025.2 or higher 

 3. Types of Tools in SAP S/4HANA and FSA 
 The integration supports two types of tools. Understanding the difference is important for both master data setup and how tools behave in the integration. 
 3.1 Generic Tools 
 A generic tool is a material that can be used as a tool on a service order but is not tracked individually by serial number. It is created as a standard material master in S/4HANA with the item category group FHMI (For full instructions go through Tools in Service Transactions - SAP Community and Product Proposals for Service Order Items | SAP Help Portal ). 
 How to create a generic tool in S/4HANA: 
 Open transaction MM01 or the SAP Fiori app "Manage Products". 
 Create a new material and set Material Type to 'Production Resource/Tool’. 
 Complete the required views (Basic Data, Prod.resources/tools and relevant plant and sales org ) and save. 

 With DRF config 194, the generic tool appears in the FSA Tools catalog. The generic tool created will act as hierarchy or category (specific set up instructions available in section 4.1). 

 3.2 Serialized Tools 
 A serialized tool is a physical asset tracked by a unique serial number. It has both a material master and an equipment master in S/4HANA, allowing full traceability of which specific unit (serial number) was used on which activity. 
 How to create a serialized tool in S/4HANA: 
 Create the equipment master using transaction IE01 (or "Create Technical Object" app in SAP Fiori), referencing the material and assigning it to the correct equipment category (example P). 
 Assign a serial number under SerData view 
 Fill any necessary data under PRT Data view 

 With Mobile Application Integration Framework, the equipment will be replicated to FSA tool catalog as serialized tool (specific set up instructions available in section 4.2). 

 4. Setup and Configuration 
 Three configuration steps are required before the integration is operational specific to tools. All three must be completed in the correct order. This set up is complimentary to instructions at Integration with SAP Field Service Management | SAP Help Portal 
 4.1 Value Mapping Configuration (For Generic Tools) 
 To enable materials to be replicated as generic tools in FSA, add a value mapping entry in ‘Value Mapping for Master Data Between SAP S/4HANA and SAP Field Service Management’ on SAP Integration Suite. In the bi-directional mapping ProductS4HANA:ProductType <-> ProductFSM:ProductType, add: 

 S/4HANA Value (Source) 
 FHMI (item category group for tool materials) 

 FSA Value (Target) 
 TOOL 

 Figure 2: Value Mapping -- FHMI mapped to TOOL 
 Note: Full setup guidance: Configure "Value Mapping for Master Data Between SAP S4HANA and SAP Field Service Management" | SAP Help Portal 
 4.2 Middleware Server Configuration (Serialized Tools) 
 To enable serialized equipment to be replicated as tools in FSA, configure the TOOL_EQUIPMENT property in the Middleware Server Management app. Under the ‘FSM Integration’ Mobile Application, add one row per equipment category that should be treated as a serialized tool: 

 Property Group 
 TOOL_EQUIPMENT 

 Property Name 
 TOOL_EQUIPMENT_CATEGORY 

 Property Value 
 Equipment category (e.g. P) -- add one row per category 

 Figure 3: Middleware Server Management -- TOOL_EQUIPMENT_CATEGORY configuration 
 Note: Full setup guidance: Define Server Management Properties | SAP Help Portal 
 4.3 iFlow Configuration -- Item Categories for FSA Tools 
 In SAP Integration Suite, open the iFlow "Replicate Service Order from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service Management SOAP" and navigate to the Configure section. Enter the item categories that should be replicated as tools to FSA: 

 iFlow 
 Replicate Service Order from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service Management SOAP 

 Parameter 
 Item Categories For FSM Tools 

 Example 
 SRVT (use pipe separator for multiple values, e.g. SRVT|SRVT2) 

 Figure 4: iFlow configuration -- Item Categories For FSM Tools set to SRVT 
 4.4 iFlow Configuration – Enable confirmations for FSA Tools 
 On iFlow "Notify Service Order Update from SAP Field Service Management to SAP S4HANA" we have configuration available to enable service confirmations for Tool usage. Mark the configuration ‘Enable Tools Confirmation Replication’ as true to post confirmations to S/4HANA. 

 This iflow also provides extension for custom logic which can be called through process direct address available under configuration ‘Tools Confirmation Extension Address’ 

 Figure 4: iFlow configuration – Enabling service confirmations with tools 
 4.5 FSA company setting to reserve tools on activity release 
 Tools assignment will always replicate as available on the activity which will be in status DRAFT. When back office releases the activity to a technician we would expect the tool to be reserved. For this FSA provides a company setting ‘CoreSystems.CoresystemsFSM.Tool.Reservation.AttemptToolBookingWhenReleasing’, setting this to true will auto reserve the tool. Even without the company setting, tools can be manually reserved using the option of reserve on web UI 

 5. Tool Assignment on a Service Order (S/4HANA) 
 Once tool master data exists in both systems, a service planner can assign tools to a service order in S/4HANA. Tool assignments are made as line items on the service order with item category "Tool item" (SRVT). These line items are replicated to the corresponding FSA activity automatically when the service order is dispatched. 
 5.1 Adding a Tool Line Item to a Service Order 
 On the service order Items tab, add a new line item and select item category SRVT (Tool item). Enter the product ID of the tool material. For serialized tools, assign the specific equipment record and serial number on the Tool Item Details tab. 

 Figure 5: S/4HANA Service Order Items tab -- Service item (CSSRV_01) and Tool item (DIGITAL_MULTIMETER) 

 Figure 6: Tool Item Details -- Equipment ID DMM01 with serial number 88768865525 assigned 
 5.2 Tool Replicated to FSA Activity (Status: Available) 
 After the service order is dispatched, the tool assignment is replicated to the FSA activity. In the FSA backoffice, the Tools tab of the activity shows the assigned tool with status "Available", confirming successful replication. 

 Figure 7: FSA Activity Tools tab -- Digital multi-meter replicated from S/4HANA (Status: Available) 
 5.3 Activity Released -- Tool Status Becomes Reserved 
 When the activity is released and a technician is assigned, the tool status automatically changes from "Available" to "Reserved", confirming that the serialized tool is allocated to this specific activity. 

 Figure 8: FSA Activity (Released) -- Tool status updated to "Reserved" 
 6. Tool Consumption in FSA (Technician View) 
 On the day of the assignment, the technician opens the FSA mobile app and navigates to their activity. The Tools section shows all tools that have been assigned from S/4HANA. Technician can consume the planned tools and also un-planned tools can be used. 
 6.1 Viewing Reserved Tools in FSA 
 The Reserved Tools screen shows the tools that were planned in S/4HANA. The technician can see the tool name and serial number before starting the job. 

 Figure 9: FSA Mobile App -- Reserved Tools showing the Digital multi-meter pre-assigned from S/4HANA 
 6.2 Consuming Tools and Adding Un-Planned Tools 
 The technician marks the reserved tool as used (by dragging and dropping the tool into ‘Used’ section) and can also add tools that were not pre-planned -- for example, a "Sinometer" that was needed on-site using ‘Add tools’ option. Both reserved and un-reserved tools appear in the Used section. This flexibility allows the actual tool consumption to be accurately captured regardless of what was planned. 

 Figure 10: FSA Mobile App -- Used Tools: Digital multi-meter (pre-assigned) + Sinometer (added on-site) 
 6.3 Closing the Activity 
 When all work is done, the technician closes the activity in FSA. This closure event triggers the confirmation posting back to S/4HANA for all consumed tools. 

 Figure 11: FSA Mobile App -- Assignment closed, triggering tool confirmation posting to S/4HANA 
 7. Confirmation Posting in S/4HANA 
 On activity closure in FSA, the tool consumption data is automatically posted to S/4HANA as a service confirmation. No manual entry is required. The confirmation captures each tool item with its equipment ID, serial number, quantity, duration, and net value -- ready for billing. 
 7.1 Confirmation Created on Service Order 

 Figure 12: S/4HANA Service Order Confirmations tab -- Confirmation 9000001492 automatically posted on activity closure 
 7.2 Confirmation Items -- Both Tools Captured 
 The confirmation items show both the pre-planned DIGITAL_MULTIMETER and the on-site SINOMETER, each with item category "Tool item Srv. Conf." and their respective net values. 

 Figure 13: Confirmation Items -- Both tool items (Digital multi-meter 120 USD + Sinometer 370 USD) posted for billing 

 Figure 14: Confirmation Item 10 -- Digital multi-meter with Equipment ID DMM01, Serial No. 88768865525 

 Figure 15: Confirmation Item 20 -- Sinometer with Equipment ID SM01, Serial No. 9925255526 
 8. Design Decisions and Key Considerations 
 8.1 Serialized Tools Only for Activity Assignment 
 FSA currently supports only serialized tools for activity tool consumption. Generic tool master data is replicated to FSA but cannot be consumed on an activity. To handle this, only serialized equipment (with a serial number) replicated into FSA activity tools. 
 Note: Ensure tool line items on S/4HANA service orders reference a serialized equipment record so they appear as tool assignments in FSA. 
 8.2 Confirmations Posted at Activity Closure Only 
 Tool consumption does not belong to the EMME (Equipment, Material, Measurement, Expense) posting category, so confirmations are not sent on intermediate saves. They are posted to S/4HANA only when the FSA activity is fully closed. 
 Note: Tool consumption data appears in S/4HANA only after the FSA activity is closed. Billing and reporting processes should account for this timing. 
 9. Summary 
 The Tool Integration between SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and SAP Field Service and Asset Management, available from 2025 FPS01, delivers: 
 Master data replication of both generic and serialized tools between S/4HANA and FSA 
 Automatic replication of serialized tool assignments from service order line items to FSA activities 
 Flexible tool consumption in the FSA mobile app -- both reserved and ad-hoc un-reserved tools 
 Automatic confirmation posting to S/4HANA on activity closure with full serial number traceability, ready for billing 
 Tools are now a first-class citizen in the end-to-end field service integration story between SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud and SAP FSA.

items.title: SAP ASE 16.1 external keystore: C_Encrypt called with zero output length fails with CKR_BUFFER_TOO_S
items.author: cleandro
items.text:
Hello, 
 I'm integrating SAP ASE with an HSM through the external keystore feature (Key Protection Using External Keystore, PKCS#11). SAP ASE can't encrypt any master key with the HSM key, and from the PKCS#11 trace the problem appears to be in how SAP ASE calls C_Encrypt. 
 Environment 
 - SAP ASE 16.1 SP00 PL02, threaded kernel mode, ASE_ENCRYPTION enabled 
 - Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 (64-bit) 
 - HSM: nShield, PKCS#11 library libcknfast.so (Security World 13.6.18) 
 Steps to reproduce 
 1. Configure the HSM credential with sp_encryption 'hsm_credential', ... (using the PKCS#11 CK_SLOT_ID). 
 2. Create the HSM key: create encryption key hsm_key for AES with keylength 256 ... external. The "SAP ASE instance key" object is created on the HSM. 
 3. Do either of the following: 
 - Migrate an existing password-protected master key: alter encryption key master modify encryption with external key 
 - Create a new master key protected by the HSM key: create encryption key master with external key 
 Expected result 
 The master key is encrypted with the HSM key. 
 Actual result 
 The operation fails. "create encryption key master with external key" returns no error to isql, but the master key isn't created. SAPASE.log shows: 
 ``` 
 kernel Call to Cryptoki API 'C_Encrypt' failed with error code 336 (0x150) CKR_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL. 
 kernel Call to Cryptoki API 'C_EncryptInit' failed with error code 144 (0x90) CKR_OPERATION_ACTIVE. 
 ``` 
 Every later HSM operation fails with CKR_OPERATION_ACTIVE until SAP ASE is restarted. 
 PKCS#11 trace 
 ``` 
 C_EncryptInit pMechanism->mechanism 0x00001085 (CKM_AES_CBC_PAD) -> CKR_OK 
 C_Encrypt pEncryptedData <non-NULL>, pData 40 bytes, *pulEncryptedDataLen 0 
 -> *pulEncryptedDataLen 48 
 -> rv 0x00000150 (CKR_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL) 
 ``` 
 SAP ASE passes a non-NULL output buffer but sets *pulEncryptedDataLen = 0. Under the PKCS#11 specification, the library correctly returns CKR_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL with the required length (48). The caller should then retry with a buffer of that size, or call with pEncryptedData = NULL first to query the length. SAP ASE doesn't retry, and the encrypt operation is left active. 
 A second observation 
 The HSM key that SAP ASE generates ("SAP ASE instance key") is a token key with CKA_SENSITIVE = false and CKA_EXTRACTABLE = true. HSMs that enforce secure key defaults reject this template (CKR_TEMPLATE_INCONSISTENT, Msg 16169) unless their security checks are relaxed. A key-protection key would normally be created with CKA_SENSITIVE = true and CKA_EXTRACTABLE = false. 
 Questions 
 1. Is this a known issue in SAP ASE 16.1 SP00 PL02, and is it fixed in a later patch level? 
 2. Is there a configuration option that makes SAP ASE pass the real output buffer size to C_Encrypt/C_Decrypt, or retry after CKR_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL? 
 3. Can the PKCS#11 template SAP ASE uses for the HSM key be configured to set CKA_SENSITIVE/CKA_EXTRACTABLE? 
 I've checked KBA 3484782 and KBA 2280166 but didn't find this behavior described. I can provide full PKCS#11 debug traces if needed. 
 Thank you.

items.title: Stable URL for a Web Client tile, and redirect URIs for a Single Page App client
items.author: AyalaKlor
items.text:
Environment: SAP Business One 10.0 FP 2608, Web Client, Extension Manager. 
 We build a single-page-app tile. The Web Client serves it from 
 https://<web client host>/extn/ui-static/<number>/<module>/index.html 
 What we observed: 
 - Updating the extension (importing a higher version over the existing one) keeps the number. 
 - Removing the extension and importing it again gives a new number. The old URL then returns 401. 
 - Within one installation, the number is the same for every company. 
 - The numbers only grow, so the number looks like a running ID per Extension Manager installation. 
 We need to link to the tile from outside it: from a UI API extension on a B1 form, from our own server, and from emails. 
 Questions: 
 1. Is the number guaranteed to stay the same across extension updates? Does it also stay the same after a B1 upgrade, a Web Client or Extension Manager reinstall, or a backup and restore? 
 2. Is the number assigned per installation, so that every customer gets a different one? 
 3. Is there a supported way to read a tile's current URL, from a script, a server, or a UI API extension? The launchpad reads it from /tcli/service/tile/tiles.svc, which is not documented. 
 4. Is there a supported URL that does not depend on this number? The launchpad code refers to /extn/ui-static/uiext/{addonUuid}/{addonPath}/. Is that path supported, and how do we find an extension's UUID? 
 5. Our current workaround is a fixed URL on our own server that redirects to the tile's current URL. Is that an acceptable pattern? 
 Redirect URI for a Single Page App client (Extension SSO Manager): 
 For sign-in from a tile, we registered a Single Page App client with the redirect URI 
 https://<web client host>/extn/ui-static/* 
 It works, and it survives a change of the number. But it matches every extension on that Web Client, not only ours. 
 6. Is this wildcard the recommended pattern for a tile? Is there a narrower pattern that matches a single extension? 
 7. Can a client hold more than one redirect URI, or be edited after it is registered? We found neither in the UI, so today each origin needs its own client. 
 Thank you.

 In W0081, we can already display the two amounts side by side for each G/L account by placing Fiscal Year of Ledger or Cost Center in Columns . What we would like to add are two calculated columns in the same table: Difference (A − B) and Percentage variance ((A − B) ÷ B × 100) . The standard Difference (%) measure compares actuals with plan. We checked Measures > Calculations > Calculate Result as and the column context menu, but could not find an option to calculate a variance between the two selected columns. 
 Could you please confirm whether the standard app supports each of the following? 
 Comparison between fiscal years for the same cost center 
 ① Difference: For the same cost center, G/L account, and fiscal period, can we add a column showing the amount for fiscal year A minus the amount for fiscal year B? 
 ② Percentage variance: Can we also add a column showing the percentage variance using fiscal year B as the denominator? For example, if the plan amounts are 90 in year A and 100 in year B, we would expect the report to show a difference of −10 and a percentage variance of −10% . 
 Comparison between cost centers for the same fiscal year and period 
 ③ Difference: For the same fiscal year, fiscal period, and G/L account, can we add a column showing the amount for cost center A minus the amount for cost center B? 
 ④ Percentage variance: Can we also add a column showing the percentage variance using cost center B as the denominator? For example, if the plan amounts are 150 for center A and 100 for center B, we would expect a difference of 50 and a percentage variance of 50% . 
 For each supported item, could you share the required settings and the steps to select the two columns and define the calculation? If any item is unsupported in the standard app, please indicate which one. Please also clarify whether the steps or available functions differ between actual-to-actual and plan-to-plan comparisons. 
 Environment: SAP S/4HANA On-Premise 2025 FPS01 (S4CORE 109 SP0001, SAP_UI 816 SP0001) 
 Query technical name shown in Query Information: 2CCFICCPLANACT2001 
 Thank you.

6.summary: A blog post, the seventh in a series, describing a Pydantic AI multi-agent application on SAP BTP. The agent was the one behind the DemoJam demo at SAP TechEd. It reads an incoming mail about an ABAP dump, uses ARC-1 to find the cause, fixes and tests the code, and replies, all in about two minutes. The excerpt is a teaser only, so the architecture, the prompts, the ARC-1 tool calls and the test approach are not shown.
key_points: The agent is built with Pydantic AI and runs as a multi-agent app on SAP BTP.
Input is an email about an ABAP short dump; output is a reply with a tested code fix.
ARC-1 is the tool the agent uses to locate the root cause of the dump.
The whole cycle is claimed to take about two minutes.
The demo was shown at SAP TechEd as DemoJam.
technical_details: Framework: Pydantic AI (multi-agent)
Platform: SAP BTP
Tooling named: ARC-1
Workflow: mail in, dump analysis, code fix, unit test, reply
No code, object names or versions are given in the excerpt
6.why_it_matters: It is a concrete example of an agent closing the loop from a production dump to a verified fix, which is the kind of workflow ABAP teams are starting to ask about. The excerpt alone does not show how reliable the fix is, so the claim should be checked against the full series.
6.teaching_angle: Use it as a discussion prompt: which steps of dump analysis (ST22 data, source location, fix, test, human review) can be delegated to an agent, and which must stay with a developer. Ask students to sketch the tool calls they would expose to such an agent.

57.summary: An introductory blog arguing that the gateway layer matters in agentic coding setups that run on SAP AI Core. The excerpt does not yet explain what the gateway is or how it should be configured.
key_points: Agentic coding tools plan, call tools, inspect results and iterate, often dozens of times in one session.
The post names five tools: Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and opencode.
The central claim is that the gateway between these tools and the model backend matters more than people expect.
The excerpt contains no configuration, code or measurements.
technical_details: Platform: SAP AI Core
Tools named: Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, opencode
No gateway product, endpoint or configuration is shown in the excerpt
57.why_it_matters: ABAP teams are beginning to run coding agents against SAP systems, and the routing layer determines cost, access control and observability. The point is valid, but this excerpt only sets up the argument.
57.teaching_angle: Use it to introduce the difference between a model and the gateway in front of it: authentication, quotas, logging and tool routing. Have students list what they would need to audit an agent that edits ABAP code.

71.summary: A question from a user whose custom fields disappeared from the field catalog of a custom RAP-based report after upgrading to what the post calls SAPUI 1.120.49. All affected fields are flagged as hidden. Turning off the hidden annotation makes the fields show again. The post does not include a reply, a CDS definition or the exact annotation used.
71.developer_problem: After a UI upgrade, custom fields disappear from the field catalog of a custom RAP report because they are flagged hidden, and removing the hidden annotation brings them back.
key_points: Custom fields vanished from the field catalog after a UI upgrade.
All affected fields carry a hidden flag.
Disabling the hidden annotation brings the fields back.
The post contains no answer and no confirmation of the root cause.
technical_details: Version as written: SAPUI 1.120.49 (the version string is probably SAPUI5 1.120.x; the post does not clarify)
Likely annotation to inspect: @UI.hidden on the CDS view entity or the metadata extension
Field catalog for a custom RAP report
71.why_it_matters: A UI upgrade changing how hidden annotations are applied would break custom reports silently. Teams need to know whether the behaviour changed in the framework or whether the fields were always wrongly annotated.
71.teaching_angle: Good debugging exercise: check where @UI.hidden is set in the CDS view or metadata extension, compare the annotation's effect before and after the upgrade, and confirm with an SAP Note or release note. Also a lesson in reporting version numbers precisely.

37.summary: A user on S/4HANA 2023 wants to merge two or more planned orders into one production order using the function module MILL_OC_ORDER_MERGE. They tried to call it from a RAP behaviour class, but the ABAP syntax check flags a violation because the function uses CALL DYNPRO internally, which is not allowed there. They ask whether another function module or a RAP business object exists for this. The post has no reply in the excerpt.
37.developer_problem: A function module that uses CALL DYNPRO cannot be called from a RAP behaviour class, and the developer needs a supported way to merge planned orders.
key_points: Goal: merge several planned orders into one production order in S/4HANA 2023.
Candidate: function module MILL_OC_ORDER_MERGE.
Blocker: the function uses CALL DYNPRO, which the RAP behaviour class context forbids.
The author asks for other function modules or a released RAP business object that does the same job.
No answer is given in the post.
technical_details: Function module: MILL_OC_ORDER_MERGE (order combination)
Release: S/4HANA 2023
Context: RAP behaviour class implementation
Restriction: CALL DYNPRO statement in called code
37.why_it_matters: Dialog-oriented function modules are common in PP and cannot be called directly from RAP, so developers need to know the released APIs or an alternative such as a wrapper with a released BAPI or a released business object. The post shows the typical trap of reusing an old dialog function from modern code.
37.teaching_angle: Use it as a case study on released versus classic APIs. Ask students to check the API state of a function module in ADT, look for released BAPIs or RAP business objects for production orders, and explain why CALL DYNPRO breaks the RAP context.

38.summary: A developer wants to build a CAP and Fiori Elements application on top of the SAP supplier quotation OData V4 service (OP_SUPPLIERQUOTATION_0001). The service does not support draft handling, so create and similar actions cannot use the draft flow Fiori Elements expects. The current idea is a CAP wrapper that adds draft capabilities and stores drafts and mirrored fields in PostgreSQL. The post links to an older thread with no solution and asks for advice; no reply is shown.
38.developer_problem: A Fiori Elements app built on CAP needs draft handling, but the supplier quotation OData V4 service does not provide it, so the developer needs a way to supply drafts.
key_points: Backing service: OP_SUPPLIERQUOTATION_0001 (OData V4, supplier quotation).
The service has no draft handling, which Fiori Elements needs for create and similar actions.
Proposed approach: a CAP wrapper adds draft behaviour and stores drafts in PostgreSQL.
Fields are mirrored from the SAP service into PostgreSQL.
The post asks for advice; no answer appears in the excerpt.
technical_details: Stack: CAP, Fiori Elements, OData V4, PostgreSQL
Remote service: OP_SUPPLIERQUOTATION_0001 on the SAP API Business Hub
Draft handling is absent on the remote service, so the wrapper must supply it
Related thread referenced for the C4C variant (no solution)
38.why_it_matters: Many released SAP OData APIs are read or write without draft, and CAP-based side-by-side apps often need to bridge that gap. The design choice (a local draft store that mirrors SAP data) carries sync and consistency risks that the post does not discuss.
38.teaching_angle: Good architecture discussion: when should a side-by-side app own draft state, how do you keep a local mirror consistent with the SAP backend, and what are the alternatives such as a Fiori Elements app with a custom action flow or a RAP-based backend? Students can compare the CAP wrapper with a RAP draft on S/4HANA.

46.summary: A blog introducing the Database Function feature of SAP Agent Lifecycle Management (ALM). ALM lets teams author, manage and synchronise SAP HANA SQLScript functions from the application without direct database access. The excerpt promises a step-by-step creation walkthrough, the required SQL format and the advantages over maintaining functions in the database, but the excerpt itself does not include those details.
key_points: SAP Agent Lifecycle Management (ALM) manages agent and producer configurations, plus contract and licensing workflows.
ALM has a built-in Database Function feature.
Functions are SAP HANA SQLScript, authored and synchronised from the application.
Teams do not need access to the database layer to do this.
The excerpt does not show the steps, the SQL format or the advantages in detail.
technical_details: Product: SAP Agent Lifecycle Management (ALM)
Feature: Database Function
Language: SAP HANA SQLScript
No object names, syntax examples or version numbers are given in the excerpt
46.why_it_matters: If agent platforms push database logic into managed functions, ABAP and data teams need to know where that logic lives, how it is versioned and who can change it. The excerpt does not give enough detail to judge that.
46.teaching_angle: Compare managed database functions with the usual approach of CDS table functions or AMDP methods in ABAP. Ask students to list the trade-offs: governance, transport, testing and performance of SQLScript outside the ABAP stack.

52.summary: A hands-on PoC in which a CAP Java service (Orders entity in OrdersService) triggers an n8n workflow on CREATE via the cds-feature-n8n plugin, using the @n8n.process.start annotation instead of custom REST code. The workflow is a Webhook node at order-created feeding a Switch node in Rules mode that routes on status (NEW vs INVALID). The author tests with two POSTs to the OData V4 endpoint and reports that each branch receives one item. The post is practical and specific about versions, but it describes plugin internals (outbox, delivery, event detection) without showing them and says nothing about failure handling or security. The text appears truncated at the production-readiness section.
key_points: Annotation-driven integration: @n8n.process.start on the entity triggers an n8n webhook on CREATE, with no custom REST client code.
Version pinning matters: the post says cds-feature-n8n needs CDS 5.2.0 and Spring Boot 4.1.2, and earlier versions fail at startup.
Two config gotchas: the N8nOutbox outbox service must be explicitly enabled, because the plugin looks up a Spring bean with that exact name.
Delivery is asynchronous via the CAP outbox; the author reports delivery within a few seconds.
Routing happens in n8n with a Switch node in Rules mode, so branching logic lives outside the Java code.
The post does not cover retries when n8n is down, webhook authentication, or what payload data leaves the system.
technical_details: Dependency com.sap.cds:cds-feature-n8n:0.0.1 added to srv/pom.xml.
Root pom properties: jdk.version 21, cds.services.version 5.2.0, spring.boot.version 4.1.2.
db/schema.cds: entity Orders with key ID : UUID, customer, product, quantity : Integer, status : String default 'NEW'.
srv/orders-service.cds: @n8n.process.start: [{ on: 'CREATE', path: 'order-created' }] on entity Orders as projection on example.Orders.
application.yaml: cds.outbox.services.N8nOutbox.enabled true; n8n.base-url http://localhost:5678.
Test: POST http://localhost:8080/odata/v4/OrdersService/Orders with status NEW and INVALID payloads.
52.why_it_matters: It shows a low-code way to connect CAP Java events to external orchestration, which is useful for trainers covering CAP extensibility. Its value depends on the reader checking plugin docs for failure and security behaviour, which the post omits.
52.developer_problem: How to trigger an external workflow from CAP Java entity events without writing custom REST or outbox code.
52.teaching_angle: Use it to discuss CAP outbox-based event delivery versus synchronous calls, and ask learners what they would add for retries, webhook auth and payload filtering before production.

22.summary: A short question asking whether a developer can use the Business One debug connection string to connect a distributed integration application to the on-premise SAP Business One v10 desktop client and its UI API. The post asks about issues if the integration is shipped to clients. It contains no answer, no error message, and no reference to documentation.
key_points: Asks whether a debug connection string is acceptable for a distributed B1 integration.
Asks about support or operational issues when shipping to customers.
No answers or official guidance are given in the thread as posted.
technical_details: SAP Business One v10, on-premise.
UI API access via the desktop application.
22.why_it_matters: The question is relevant to anyone shipping B1 add-ons, because using a debug or development connection path in production is a supportability and licensing risk. The post itself gives no technical answer.
22.developer_problem: Whether a debug connection string is suitable for a distributed Business One integration that uses UI API.
22.teaching_angle: Use it to teach the difference between development and production connection setup, and to check the vendor's supported connection and licensing guidance before shipping.

30.summary: Asks how to get SAP Business One Web Client extension files under /extn/ui-static/ to cache and compress. The author reports Cache-Control no-cache and no-store, no ETag, and no Content-Encoding on FP 2608. They note their build uses content-hashed file names, so long-term caching would be safe for everything except index.html. The post asks where the settings live and what SAP recommends.
key_points: Extension files are served with Cache-Control no-cache, no-store, no ETag and no Content-Encoding.
Every tile open re-downloads all files uncompressed.
The build already uses content-hashed file names, which the author says makes long-term caching safe except for index.html.
Three open questions: can caching be enabled, where is it configured, and what does SAP recommend.
technical_details: Environment: SAP Business One 10.0 FP 2608, Web Client.
Path prefix: /extn/ui-static/.
Headers observed: Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store; no ETag; no Content-Encoding.
30.why_it_matters: Slow tile loads are a common complaint with SPA extensions, and the headers reported here work against caching. The post shows the right reasoning (hashed assets, index.html excluded) but has no answer yet.
30.developer_problem: Why Web Client extension assets are not cached or compressed, and how to change that.
30.teaching_angle: Use it to teach Cache-Control semantics (no-cache versus no-store versus immutable with max-age), ETag revalidation, and content-hashed asset strategy with an index.html exception.

31.summary: Asks for an official list of UI API view and control GUIDs for Business One Web Client extensions. The author takes baseViewGuid values from the VS Code plugin manifest schema, notes that some look like placeholders (two down-payment invoice views share one GUID), and uses control GUIDs of the form UDF_<TABLE>_<UDF> inferred from a sample. They say the GUIDs stayed the same across FP 2602, 2605 and 2608. They ask about the guarantee for UDF naming and SAP's compatibility policy.
key_points: No API returns view GUIDs; the author relies on the VS Code plugin manifest schema suggestions.
Some baseViewGuid values look like placeholders; two down-payment invoice views share one GUID.
Header UDF control GUID pattern UDF_<TABLE>_<UDF> works but was inferred from a sample.
Schema allows 8 to 32 characters after UDF_, which the author flags as a risk for long UDF names.
GUIDs were stable across FP 2602, 2605 and 2608.
technical_details: Environment: SAP Business One 10.0 FP 2608, UI API extensions.
Manifest schema from the VS Code plugin for Web Client supplies baseViewGuid suggestions.
Web Client Inspector is the only pointer given in the guide.
Control GUID format UDF_<TABLE>_<UDF>; length constraint 8 to 32 after UDF_.
31.why_it_matters: Hard-coded GUIDs are the main upgrade risk for UI API extensions. The post shows that undocumented identifiers are being used in production, so each feature pack should be regression-tested.
31.developer_problem: How to find the authoritative view and control GUIDs for UI API extensions and whether the UDF naming pattern is guaranteed.
31.teaching_angle: Use it to teach the risk of relying on undocumented identifiers, and how to verify them through the Inspector and regression tests per feature pack.

32.summary: Describes a single-page-app Web Client tile (deploy_mode b1-webclient) whose URL changes on every upload, from /extn/ui-static/<number>/<module>/index.html. The old path returns 401, which breaks UDF links, bookmarks and cross-tile links. The number is shared by all companies in an installation. The author found an alternative uiext/{addonUuid}/{addonPath} form in launchpad code and asks whether it is supported, how to find the UUID, and whether the number is stable across upgrades or restores.

digest.headline: Thin ABAP day: RAP and function-module limits, an AUTHORITY-CHECK puzzle, agent-for-dumps teasers, and unanswered Business One questions.
digest.overview:
Today's material is mostly unanswered questions and teaser blogs. The ABAP-relevant items are a RAP report losing custom fields after a UI upgrade (71), a dialog function module that cannot be called from a RAP behaviour class (37), a Brazil PO BAPI/BAdI problem (83) and an AUTHORITY-CHECK with an empty field value (85). Two AI blogs cover an agent that fixes ABAP dumps and the gateway layer for coding agents (6, 57). Both excerpts lack technical detail.

No post gives a confirmed answer, so treat every cause as a hypothesis to verify in a system. The value for teaching lies in the problem patterns: released versus classic APIs, annotation behaviour after upgrades, and exact matching of authorization values.

deep_dives.title: Calling classic function modules from RAP: released APIs and CALL DYNPRO
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (37) describes calling MILL_OC_ORDER_MERGE from a RAP behaviour class on S/4HANA 2023. The syntax check complains because the function uses CALL DYNPRO. The post gives no answer, so the following is general reasoning, not a confirmed fix.

In ABAP Cloud-style development, code may only use released APIs. In ADT, open the function module and check its API state in the properties (the API State tab). Dialog-oriented modules are normally not released. If the strict language version applies to the behaviour class, the check will reject them. In a standard-ABAP behaviour class, the restriction may come from the RAP context, where dialog processing is not permitted at all.

Options to evaluate: look for a released BAPI or a released business object for production orders or planned order conversion; ask SAP via an influence request or search for released CDS/RAP APIs; or wrap the classic logic in a separate unreleased class used only in a tier where classic ABAP is allowed, called through a clearly isolated interface. A dialog function that relies on screens may not work outside a dialog session even if the call compiled, so test it with batch input style alternatives only as a last resort.

Teach students to check the API state first, then search released objects, before writing a wrapper.

deep_dives.title: AUTHORITY-CHECK with empty values
deep_dives.explanation:
Post 85 asks why a custom authorization object field with a blank value still gives SY-SUBRC 4. Role data, the call and SU53 are missing, so the cause is unconfirmed. This is a checklist.

First, see what the role really holds. In PFCG, a field with no value maintained is not the same as a field holding a literal blank. The ' ' typed in a source field of the object is not a role value. Check the role's authorization data for the object and confirm the field has an entry.

Second, see what is passed. AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'ZOBJ' ID 'ZFIELD' FIELD lv_value compares the value of lv_value against the role. An initial character variable and the literal ' ' are both a blank in ABAP, but the role must contain a matching entry. If the field should be skipped, the check can use ID 'ZFIELD' DUMMY, which disables the check for that field.

Third, run the check, then open SU53. It shows which object, fields and values were checked and what the user holds. Compare them.

deep_dives.title: Hidden annotations after a UI upgrade in a custom RAP report
deep_dives.explanation:
In post 71, custom fields in a RAP report disappeared from the field catalog after a UI upgrade. All were flagged hidden and removing the hidden annotation restored them. No cause is confirmed.

The likely place to look is @UI.hidden in the CDS view entity or a metadata extension. Fields added through custom field extensibility may get annotations generated by the tool, so check the generated extension too. Also check whether the annotation is static (true) or driven by a path to another field, since the evaluation could differ between versions.

A practical method: read the effective annotations for the entity in ADT, compare with a system before the upgrade, then check the UI5 release notes and SAP Notes for the stated version. The version string in the post may not be exactly SAPUI5 1.120.x, so confirm it first.

interview_questions.question: A RAP behaviour class must reuse a classic function module that uses CALL DYNPRO. How do you approach it?
interview_questions.answer: First, check the module's API release state in ADT, since unreleased and dialog-based modules are not allowed under ABAP Cloud-style rules. Then search for a released BAPI, CDS view or RAP business object that does the same job. If none exists, consider an isolated wrapper in a context where classic ABAP is allowed, with a clear interface. A function that depends on screens may not run correctly outside a dialog session, so it must be tested. I would also consider requesting a released API from SAP. Avoid hiding the dependency, because it will break on upgrade or in a cloud move.

interview_questions.question: AUTHORITY-CHECK returns SY-SUBRC 4 for a custom object field that should allow an empty value. What do you check?
interview_questions.answer: Start with PFCG and confirm the role holds an entry for that field. Not maintained is different from a blank. Next confirm what the program passes in FIELD, and compare with SU53, which shows the checked values. If the field should not be checked in a given call, use ID 'FIELD' DUMMY. Also confirm the user's authorizations were refreshed after the role change. Finally verify that the object definition in SU21 matches the call's field names.

interview_questions.question: After a UI upgrade, custom fields disappear from a RAP-based report and are flagged hidden. How do you investigate?
interview_questions.answer: I would first confirm the exact UI5 and backend versions. Then read the effective annotations of the entity in ADT, including metadata extensions and annotations generated for custom fields. I look for @UI.hidden, whether static or path-based. I compare with a system before the upgrade and read the release notes and SAP Notes. Removing the annotation is a workaround, not a diagnosis. A regression test of the field list after each upgrade would catch it earlier.
